KUALA LUMPUR – The seizure of 521kg of methamphetamine aboard a private jet in Laos on Oct 1 did not originate from Malaysia, but was instead suspected to be smuggled from that country to the Philippines.
Bukit Aman Narcotics Crime Investigation Department (NCID) director Hussein Omar Khan said based on information from the Laotian authorities, the chartered aircraft departed from Sultan Abdul Aziz Shah Airport in Subang to Luang Prabang without carrying any cargo.
He said the flight from Subang carried only three individuals comprising a Singaporean pilot, a Malaysian co-pilot, and a Filipino passenger.
“The seized drugs were meant for the Manila market in the Philippines and not the Malaysian market. The aircraft departed from Subang Airport without any cargo before it was believed to have been used to transport the drug shipment from Laos to Manila,” he said in a statement.
Elaborating on the timeline shared by Laotian authorities, he said the private aircraft arrived at Luang Prabang International Airport at about 11.30am local time on Oct 1.
“At 1.30 pm, two vehicles arrived at the airport area, and several airport staff subsequently assisted in transferring 23 bags from the vehicles onto trolleys to be loaded onto the aircraft.
“An inspection of all 23 bags uncovered 500 packages of drugs suspected to be methamphetamine weighing 521kg,” he said.

articles.summary: Thailand, US writing ‘final paragraph’ of trade deal, says PM Anutin  CNAThailand at ‘last paragraph’ of US trade agreement: PM Anutin  The Business TimesTrump hopes to sign Thai tariff deal during November Asia visit  The StarThailand at 'last paragraph' of US trade agreement, PM says, Asia News  AsiaOneThailand-US trade surges as both sides move closer to tariff deal  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul received a letter from US President Donald Trump last week confirming both countries were “at the final stage” on the agreement, he said at a forum in Singapore on Wednesday (Oct 7).
SINGAPORE: Thailand is “at the last paragraph” of its Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States and could sign the deal on US President Donald Trump’s next visit to Asia, said Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul on Wednesday (Oct 7).
Anutin received a letter from Trump last week confirming both countries were “at the final stage” on the agreement, he said at a dialogue with Forbes Media chairman and editor-in-chief Steve Forbes.
“(Trump) told me I was to make sure that my people and the US Trade Representative would write up the final clause, and he expected we could sign the agreement … in the letter, he said, ‘on my next visit to Asia’,” Anutin told attendees at the gala dinner of the Forbes Global CEO Conference at the Shangri-La Singapore hotel.
Trump is expected to visit Asia in November to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in the Philippines and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen.
Thai exports to the US are currently subject to a 12.5 per cent tariff related to forced-labour measures. A separate investigation into production overcapacity is pending. The US is Thailand’s largest export market.
This was up from a temporary 10 per cent tariff that had expired in July.
Thailand has a sizeable goods trade surplus with the US, which reached US$71.7 billion in 2025, according to the Office of the US Trade Representative. That was up 59.1 per cent from 2024.
In services, however, the US recorded a US$15 million trade surplus with Thailand in 2025, reversing a US$5 million deficit in 2024.
However, Thailand has a substantial trade deficit with China.
When asked by Forbes about this, Anutin said he was “sure that the level of deficit with China will greatly, greatly reduce with time” due to Chinese investments flowing into his country.
Thailand’s trade deficit with China has widened by 59.3 per cent in the first seven months of this year, amounting to US$55.13 billion, Thai news outlet The Nation reported in September.
Anutin said Thailand has had “numerous projects from China as direct investment” since the beginning of this year.
He also met with automobile players during his visit to China in July, “where they confirmed their investments into our country”, said Anutin.
Making a case for investing in Thailand, Anutin said that after taking office in September 2025, he, together with Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow, vowed to put Thailand on the “radar” to bring in more innovative businesses.
In discussions with foreign investors, he “begged” them not to see Thailand as a country of “cheap labour supply, cheap facilities, cheap utility charges”, but as a place with developed logistics and communications systems, and a distribution hub for ASEAN and beyond, he said.
He was able to meet foreign dignitaries through the ASEAN and APEC summits, and a ceasefire agreement signed with Cambodia last October in the presence of Trump and Malaysia Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim in Kuala Lumpur meant “we are in the focus of (the) media”, he said.
Tensions with Cambodia over a disputed border area erupted into military clashes earlier last year. The flare-up claimed at least 43 lives and displaced more than 300,000 people from both sides of the border.
Thailand is seeking membership in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) to assure investors it is a “reliable place” to put their money in, he said. The OECD is an international organisation of mainly advanced economies that develops policy standards and advice on how countries can better run their economies, institutions and public services.
When asked by Forbes about Thailand’s role in taking in refugees from Myanmar and other parts of the region, Anutin said Thai people “have no problems in helping friends in need” and believe in “humanitarian prosperity”.

articles.title: Myanmar pushes back on ASEAN envoy and call to free Suu Kyi - Awani International
articles.summary: Myanmar pushes back on ASEAN envoy and call to free Suu Kyi  Awani International
articles.full_text:
MYANMAR'S military-backed government has pushed back against the regional ASEAN bloc's special envoy for the war-torn country, days after its leader made a landmark visit to Thailand, which is pushing for its neighbour's full re-engagement with the grouping.
The relationship between Myanmar and the 11-member Association for Southeast Asian Nations has been strained since early 2021 when the military leader ousted an elected civilian government led by Aung San Suu Kyi, sparking a nationwide civil war that has killed an estimated 100,000 people and displaced millions.
Myanmar's leadership has since been banned from top-level ASEAN meetings over their failure to implement a "five-point consensus" peace plan agreed with the bloc.
In a weekend statement, Myanmar's foreign ministry said an ASEAN special envoy for Myanmar was no longer needed, pointing to an election held around the turn of the year.
"Myanmar is of the view that the appointment and the continued role of the new special envoy of the ASEAN chair are no longer necessary," the statement said.
The widely criticised election held in December and January was won by a military-backed party in the absence of any substantial opposition, allowing Myanmar's then junta leader Min Aung Hlaing to transition to become the country's president.
After talks with Min Aung Hlaing in Bangkok last week, Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said that Thailand wants peace and stability in Myanmar as part of ASEAN's peace plan and is not abandoning regional concerns.
However, Myanmar's pro-military parliament last month passed a motion rejecting ASEAN's plan, calling it interference and adding that ASEAN should reassess its position on the country.
SUU KYI DETENTION
The foreign ministry statement followed one issued by ASEAN on Friday, which noted a meeting last week between Suu Kyi and an International Committee of the Red Cross official.
Friday's ASEAN statement also reiterated the bloc's desire for the current ASEAN envoy — the Philippine foreign minister — to meet with Suu Kyi and called for her unconditional release, alongside other political prisoners.
The 81-year-old Nobel Peace Prize winner is currently serving an 18-year sentence for a series of offences she denies committing, with no foreign leader or envoy having publicly met her until last week's meeting with the ICRC representative.
In response to ASEAN's position on Suu Kyi, the Myanmar foreign ministry said: "Although the government has commuted her sentences based on humanitarian considerations, the matter of a full and unconditional release shall only be carried out in accordance with the law."

articles.title: Singapore to seek deeper ASEAN integration, wider partnerships as 2027 chair - The Online Citizen
articles.summary: Singapore to seek deeper ASEAN integration, wider partnerships as 2027 chair  The Online Citizen
articles.full_text:
Foreign Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan said Singapore will push for deeper ASEAN economic integration and partnerships beyond traditional dialogue partners when it chairs the bloc in 2027, while warning of US-China rivalry, threats to transit passage and risks from AI.
- Singapore will pursue deeper ASEAN integration and partnerships beyond traditional dialogue partners as 2027 chair.
- Dr Balakrishnan said Singapore will refuse to choose between the US and China while maintaining trust with both.
- He warned that autonomous AI agents pose real loss-of-control and weapons proliferation risks.
Singapore will seek deeper economic integration within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and wider partnerships beyond the bloc's traditional dialogue partners when it takes up the chairmanship in 2027, Minister for Foreign Affairs Dr Vivian Balakrishnan said on Wednesday, 7 October 2026.
He was speaking at a fireside chat at the Milken Institute Asia Summit 2026, held at the Four Seasons Hotel in Singapore and moderated by Milken Institute chief executive Richard Ditizio.
Asked what would make Singapore's chairmanship a success, Dr Balakrishnan said ASEAN would have succeeded if its economy continued to grow and integrate, and if members' strengths in areas such as energy and technology became complementary.
"The more we can raft our economies, the better we can cope with high waves and strong winds," he told an audience of business, finance and government leaders.
Partnerships beyond traditional dialogue partners
Dr Balakrishnan said the wider partnerships would extend to the European Union, Africa, South America, the Pacific Islands and Canada, which he described as part of a "Trans-Pacific strategy".
He said that, apart from Indonesia, ASEAN members are small by definition and are navigating turbulent conditions together.
By cumulative nominal gross domestic product, ASEAN is or may already be the world's fourth-largest composite economy, he said, with great growth potential over the next 20 years.
"We want to be assessed on our own merit, not as an arena for contestation between the superpowers, and not as another arena for proxy wars," he said.
He cited first-half 2026 growth figures: Vietnam at over 8 per cent, Singapore at 6.1 per cent, and Malaysia and Indonesia at around 5 per cent or more.
He also said Taiwan was Singapore's largest trading partner in 2025, displacing China, and attributed much of the shift to artificial intelligence (AI), semiconductors and technology.
The Philippines currently holds ASEAN's rotating chairmanship. CNA reported that it is expected to host a summit next month, which typically concludes with a ceremonial handover to the incoming chair.
CNA also noted that Singapore accounts for about one in 10 chips made worldwide, and that VSMC, a Taiwanese-Dutch joint venture, opened an S$8.5 billion wafer fabrication plant in Singapore in September.
Domestic politics behind global disruption
Asked how middle powers and small states can navigate geopolitics and emerging technology, Dr Balakrishnan said the United States had for decades underwritten globalisation and international rules, "although sometimes hypocritically".
He said the key change was domestic politics in both superpowers: inequality and polarisation in the US, and in China, demographic decline and an imbalance between consumption and export-led production.
Until domestic politics rebalance and a new world order emerges, "we are going to be in unsettled times", he said. Outward-oriented economies such as Singapore, where trade is three times GDP, must now plan on a "just in case" basis.
Trust as Singapore's premium
Ditizio asked whether Singapore, with its high trust factor, could help shape how technologies are adopted and regulated. Dr Balakrishnan cited former US Secretary of State George Shultz's remark that trust is "the coin of the realm".
He said Singapore would "double down" on its trust premium by not panicking in crises, never confiscating properly earned wealth, upholding sanctity of contract, applying laws consistently and maintaining sufficient transparency.
He added that governments must be upfront with citizens about trade-offs, calling this "the missing ingredient" in many political systems that leads to "the corrosive erosion of trust".
Refusing to choose between Washington and Beijing
Dr Balakrishnan described US-China rivalry as a "peculiarly sensitive and existential point" for Singapore, which depends on trust to attract investment and assets.
He recounted telling the US President that American foreign direct investment stock in Southeast Asia exceeded that in India, China, Japan and Korea combined, noting that more than half of it is in Singapore.
On China, he said Singapore is the only political entity where 74 per cent of the population has Chinese ancestry. Chinese counterparts, he said, often suggest Singapore should understand them best, which in effect means "you should agree with us".
"As long and as far as we can do so, we will refuse to choose, because the moment you choose, you have lost strategic options and strategic latitude," he said.
He said Singapore would not be used by either power "as a proxy or as a lever", and would aim to be useful to both without being "made use of".
Rejecting the idea of strict balance, he said he preferred "a clear, steady, principled, consistent position", so that any refusal is understood as based on Singapore's own long-term national interest rather than siding with the other power.
Strait of Hormuz and transit passage
Ditizio referred to Dr Balakrishnan's recent United Nations speech, in which he said the closure of the Strait of Hormuz violated the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and must be collectively rejected.
Dr Balakrishnan said about 40 per cent of global trade passes through the Straits of Malacca and Singapore, which are about two nautical miles wide at their narrowest point.
Singapore earns value by providing services rather than collecting tolls, he said, and any "full-frontal assault" on the right of transit passage is "a full-frontal threat to our business model".
He recounted an unnamed Gulf counterpart saying his country was earning more than before the war by running a "Hormuz shuttle" of very large crude carriers and self-insuring against attacks.
He cautioned that the Bab al-Mandeb Strait was also at risk. If Iran were allowed to charge tolls, he said, it would gain a veto over passage and strategic dominance, which he doubted the US or Gulf states would accept.
Global rules still possible
Asked whether rules that every country follows can still be built, he said yes, "but with greater difficulty", citing the Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ) Treaty, concluded by consensus under Singaporean diplomat Ambassador Rena Lee.
According to The Straits Times, the treaty was adopted in 2023 and came into force on 17 January 2026 after ratification by more than 80 nations.
Dr Balakrishnan said similar frameworks are needed for space, AI and biotechnology. "If you want to move fast, you also need to have good brakes," he said.
He likened the present to the start of "another gilded age", recalling the railway boom of the last industrial revolution, which brought both great investments and great volatility.
Warning on AI agents
Reflecting on some 11 years as foreign minister, Dr Balakrishnan said the promise of AI was not obvious in 2015. He said he had built his own AI agents and had concluded "we have a real problem".
"Anyone who tells you, 'I've got absolute control over my autonomous agent, and I know exactly everything it is going to do or not do', obviously does not know what he is talking about. Loss of control is a real threat," he said.
He warned that rogue state and non-state actors could use the technology to develop new weapons in chemistry or biology, and flagged its impact on belief, cooperation and the practice of politics.
He said AI agents trained on internet content, much of which he described as "violent, misogynistic, unfair, crazy", should be expected to reflect humanity. "Now that can either be very scary, or it should be a moment of great contemplation," he said.
CNA noted that his remarks echoed recent warnings, including a 23 September briefing to the UN Security Council by leaders from Anthropic, OpenAI and Hugging Face, and a September call by Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and more than 20 world leaders for AI safety measures.

articles.title: Beyond tariffs: The US–Turkey trade relationship needs a bigger bargain - Atlantic Council
articles.summary: Beyond tariffs: The US–Turkey trade relationship needs a bigger bargain  Atlantic Council
articles.full_text:
Turkey has much of what the United States wants from an economic-security partner, combining a strong manufacturing base with strategic geography and regional influence. Yet it faces a comparatively high tariff burden, and new risks stemming from its energy relationships with Russia and Iran.
The tension reflects a broader change in how Washington is using tariffs: not only to protect domestic industries, but to encourage trading partners to invest in the United States, align with US regulatory and economic-security priorities, and build more secure supply chains. The result is a trade system in which market access increasingly depends on a country’s contribution to US industrial and economic-security goals.
For Ankara, that means thinking beyond tariff relief. For Washingon, Turkey’s industrial capacity, strategic location, and access to important regional markets create the opportunity to turn a difficult trade relationship into an economic security partnership. A structured bargain linking tariff relief to greater bilateral trade, investment, and supply-chain security could advance the two countries’ longstanding $100 billion trade goal while deepening cooperation in strategically important sectors.
The evolution of US trade policy toward Turkey
During President Donald Trump’s first term, Section 232 tariffs on steel and aluminum, Section 301 tariffs on Chinese goods, and the renegotiation of the North American Free Trade Agreement into the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement laid the foundation for an America First trade policy that, by the start of Trump’s second term, had evolved into a more integrated strategy linking trade policy with national security.
Turkey entered this environment through Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962. In 2018, Turkish steel initially faced a 50 percent rate before reverting to 25 percent in 2019. In 2025, the United States expanded Section 232 coverage and raised the general steel and aluminum tariff rate to 50 percent before further restructuring the metals regime in 2026. Turkey exports more than $1 billion of steel annually to the United States, making steel a major source of friction.
Washington has since broadened both the legal authorities it uses and the objectives tariffs are intended to serve. In April 2025, a 10 percent tariff was imposed on Turkey as part of the initial “Liberation Day” tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), then the lowest rate applied to any major US trade partner. After the US Supreme Court invalidated the IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, the White House imposed a temporary 10 percent import surcharge under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974. The administration then turned to a broader use of Section 301 of the Trade Act.
In July, the US Trade Representative (USTR) finalized tariffs under its forced-labor investigations covering sixty economies, including Turkey, for not having imposed and effectively enforced strong enough prohibitions on goods produced with forced labor. Economies that adopted, or committed to adopt, qualifying controls received a 10 percent rate. Turkey and most other investigated economies received a 12.5 percent rate. Notably, Turkey was not among the sixteen economies potentially subject to additional tariffs under a second Section 301 investigation into structural industrial excess capacity.
Turkey’s strategic value and economic security exposure
Several major US trade partners, including Japan, the European Union, South Korea, and Switzerland, have negotiated arrangements that cap their combined most-favored-nation and forced-labor Section 301 tariff burden at 10 percent or 12.5 percent. Turkey has no comparable arrangement.
Exposure also varies by product. Goods already covered by Section 232 are generally excluded from the forced-labor Section 301 tariffs, while products outside the Section 232 regime may instead fall under the new Section 301 tariffs. Ordinary customs duties and, for certain products, antidumping or countervailing duties can raise the final cost even further.
Furthermore, Turkey’s exposure increasingly extends beyond traditional tariff policy. The Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 allows for tariffs of up to 100 percent on imports from certain major purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas, potentially including Turkey, in addition to other applicable tariffs.
Iran poses an additional challenge because Turkey has historically balanced its strong commercial and energy connections with Iran against US sanctions. On September 4, the Treasury Department sanctioned a Turkish financial institution and two affiliates, accusing them of helping Iran evade sanctions and manage oil revenue.
At the same time, Turkey’s industrial base and geography give it potential value to US economic security objectives. Its economy spans automotive production, machinery, aerospace and defense, steel, energy equipment, and advanced manufacturing, while its integration into European value chains gives Turkish firms experience in sophisticated production networks. Its location also provides commercial connectivity across the Black Sea, the Caucasus, Central Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa, positioning it as a potential partner in US efforts to diversify strategic supply chains and reduce dependencies.
That potential spans across sectors vital to Washington’s economic security agenda. Turkey could contribute in areas such as critical minerals, energy, defense, advanced manufacturing, infrastructure, and regional logistics. Closer economic ties would not eliminate Turkey’s strategic independence or ensure alignment with US policies, but they could deepen cooperation on shared priorities, including energy and trade routes, infrastructure, and regional economic projects.
The opportunity for a broader US–Turkey bargain
In 2025, US–Turkey goods trade reached about $36.8 billion, including a roughly $4 billion US surplus in 2025. Overall trade in goods and services has more than doubled since 2019, when Trump and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan established a target of $100 billion in bilateral trade, but remains well short of that ambition.
Turkey has no reciprocal trade agreement that offers a clear path toward preferential tariff treatment or deeper economic cooperation. For Ankara, tariff relief should therefore form part of a broader negotiating agenda. Turkey could offer greater market access for US companies, address longstanding trade tensions, strengthen customs and supply-chain enforcement, and deepen regulatory cooperation in exchange for more predictable tariff treatment. An interim trade arrangement, potentially drawing on elements of US agreements with Taiwan and Indonesia, could provide a framework for addressing these issues while building toward a deeper economic relationship.
Turkey’s Digital Services Tax (DST) illustrates the potential bargaining space. USTR previously found the tax discriminatory and burdensome to US commerce, but Turkey later agreed to remove it once the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development Pillar One framework entered into force, prompting USTR to terminate its planned retaliatory tariffs. With that process unresolved, Turkey has instead begun phasing down the tax, from 7.5 percent to 5 percent in 2026 and 2.5 percent in 2027.
Addressing the DST would not directly affect Turkey’s 12.5 percent forced-labor tariff, but could remove a source of friction in broader negotiations. USTR’s July 2026 Section 301 action against Brazil shows that digital trade concerns remain part of Washington’s reciprocal trade and enforcement agenda.
Washington, in turn, should consider what it can offer. Tariff accommodations (including on Section 232 steel tariffs) along with improved market access and targeted US financing and investment could draw Turkey more deeply into trusted US supply chains while encouraging domestic and allied sourcing.
The administration has already shown willingness to calibrate tariffs where they could undermine broader economic security objectives, including through exclusions for selected raw materials and domestically unavailable inputs. Targeted accommodations could similarly support US industrial and supply-chain objectives.
Turkey’s comparative advantage in such a bargain would not be in matching the scale of US investment pledges made by Japan or South Korea. It would be its industrial capacity, geographic reach, and ability to support diversification across strategically important regions.
Steel offers an obvious place to test that proposition, but any accommodation would also require confronting global excess capacity and transshipment risks. Turkey’s participation in the September 2026 Global Forum on Steel Excess Capacity provides a potential foundation for addressing those concerns alongside the United States and other major steel-producing economies.
Any deeper economic partnership could therefore be reciprocal, though not symmetrical. Turkey can offer greater market access, regulatory cooperation, supply-chain safeguards, sourcing transparency, and access to industrial and regional networks. The United States can offer capital, technology, financing, strategic investment, and potentially more favorable tariff treatment.
A structured US–Turkey economic security partnership could bring these elements together and provide a more concrete framework for their shared trade ambitions while lowering economic frictions, enhancing Turkey’s integration into US and allied supply chains, and reinforcing shared interests across strategically important regions.
Leo Ayala is a vice president for global trade and supply chains at a Washington, DC-based geopolitical advisory firm. He previously served as an international trade specialist in the Office of Europe and Eurasia at the US Department of Commerce. The views expressed are his own.

articles.title: Why Indonesia Is Weighing a Moratorium on Semi-Finished Nickel Smelters - Tempo.co English
articles.summary: Why Indonesia Is Weighing a Moratorium on Semi-Finished Nickel Smelters  Tempo.co English
articles.full_text:
October 7, 2026 | 07:06 pm
TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - Indonesia is considering a moratorium on the development of nickel smelters that produce semi-finished products amid growing concerns over a global nickel oversupply, Coordinating Minister for Energy Transition and Downstreaming and Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Bahlil Lahadalia said.
Bahlil raised the possibility while speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the Investor Daily Summit in Jakarta on Wednesday.
He said most of Indonesia’s operating nickel smelters still produce semi-finished products, accounting for around 50 to 60 percent of output. The government is concerned that nickel supply has already exceeded global market demand.
The global nickel oversupply has reached around 2.5 million tons, putting downward pressure on international nickel prices, Bahlil said.
“There is an oversupply, which is why prices are falling. We can consider minimizing the development of semi-finished product industries, and may even impose a temporary moratorium. What we want to promote instead are industries that directly produce downstream products,” Bahlil said.
Indonesia Reviews Its Nickel Industry Strategy
Bahlil said the government is reviewing the direction of Indonesia’s nickel industry and that not all nickel processing industries producing semi-finished products need to continue receiving government support.
Indonesia’s main semi-finished nickel products include ferronickel, nickel pig iron (NPI), nickel matte and mixed hydroxide precipitate (MHP).
The government will assess which industries should continue and which should have their development restricted. One option under discussion is a moratorium on industries producing semi-finished nickel products.
“We will report this to the President, Prabowo Subianto, but in my discussions with the team, it is important that we start deciding which industries should continue and which should be subject to a moratorium, so that we do not manage our natural resources recklessly,” Bahlil said.
He said the policy is needed to ensure that Indonesia’s nickel resources are managed not only with a focus on increasing processing capacity, but also with consideration for the sustainability of reserves and the structure of the national industry.
Government to Prioritize Downstream Products
Bahlil said the moratorium would be considered particularly if global markets continued to face an oversupply of semi-finished nickel products.
He said current supply and reserve conditions had put further pressure on nickel prices.
“If there is already an oversupply in the global market, and now we have 2.5 million tons relative to demand and reserves, this is an oversupply, which is why prices are falling,” Bahlil said.
The government will also assess the possibility of limiting additional capacity for industries that only produce semi-finished products, while giving greater priority to industries capable of producing finished downstream products directly.
“What we want to promote are industries that directly produce downstream products, so that we can truly shift the structure of our economy,” Bahlil said.

articles.full_text:
| SBV officials address the press conference. — VNS Photo | 
HÀ NỘI — Total outstanding loans across the banking system hit nearly VNĐ20.75 quadrillion (US$786 billion) as of September 30 this year significantly supporting Việt Nam’s high GDP growth target, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) Phạm Thanh Hà said at a press conference on Thursday.
Speaking at the event to reveal the banking sector's performance in the first nine months of 2026 and outline steps for the remaining months of the year, Hà said that the credit increased by 11.59 per cent compared to the end of 2025 and 16.69 per cent year-on-year.
The results, he said, were due to effective measures taken by the SBV and commercial banks amid the difficulties in the global market.
“The SBV has implemented appropriate measures to help control inflation, stabilise the macro-economy, and support economic growth," Hà said.
"Notably, it has promptly directed credit institutions to implement credit solutions for specific sectors and industries, thereby facilitating access to credit for businesses and the public, especially large-scale and key projects.”
Nguyễn Xuân Bắc, deputy director of the SBV’s Credit Department, reported that bank credit structure in the first three quarters aligned with the economic sector structure.
“Credit capital continued to be channeled into production, business, and priority sectors," Bắc said.
"As of the end of August 2026, credit proportion to agriculture, forestry, and fisheries accounted for 6.08 per cent; industry and construction accounted for 23.1 per cent; and trade and services accounted for 70.11 per cent.”
“Priority sectors designated by the Government and the Prime Minister accounted for a significant share, such as agriculture and rural development at approximately 22 per cent; or sectors that gained high growth rates, such as exports with 33.32 per cent and high-tech enterprises with 39.62 per cent,” Bắc added.
Regarding interest rates, Hà said that the SBV continued to maintain benchmark interest rates, creating favourable conditions for credit institutions to access capital from the SBV at low costs, enabling them to support the economy.
The average interest rate for new deposits as of September 20 this year stood at 6.38 per cent per annum, an increase of 1.15 percentage points compared to the end of 2025.
Despite the rise, Hà noted that, the rising pace is slowing, and interest rate levels are essentially stabilising around a new baseline.
According to Phạm Chí Quang, director of the SBV’s Monetary Department, although the exchange rate and foreign exchange market have been under pressure from recent unpredictable global developments, the SBV managed the exchange rate flexibly, helping to absorb external shocks.
Effective coordination between monetary policy tools helped stabilise the foreign exchange market, contributing to macro-economic stability and inflation control. As a result, the foreign exchange market is operating smoothly, the legitimate foreign currency needs of the economy are being fully and promptly met, and the USD-VNĐ exchange rate is fluctuating flexibly, in accordance with market conditions, Quang said.
In the remaining months of the year, Hà said that the SBV will continue to flexibly manage monetary policy, closely coordinating with fiscal policy and other macro-economic measures to control inflation, contribute to macro-economic stability and support sustainable economic growth.
Interest rates will be managed in line with market developments, macro-economic conditions, inflation and monetary policy objectives. The central bank will also continue to closely monitor developments in deposit and lending interest rates for the market and for each credit institution.
"The SBV will continue to closely monitor international and domestic market developments," Hà added.
"It will manage exchange rates flexibly, in accordance with market conditions, and coordinate with other monetary policy tools to stabilise the foreign exchange market, contributing to macro-economic stability, controlling inflation and supporting economic growth." — VNS/BIZHUB

articles.summary: Myanmar Junta Leader Visits Malaysia for Repatriation Talks Amid Human Rights Backlash  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
Myanmar’s military-backed leader, Min Aung Hlaing, has embarked on a controversial diplomatic visit to Malaysia to negotiate the repatriation of thousands of Myanmar nationals. The two-day official visit, which commenced on Wednesday, underscores a complex regional dialogue as the two Southeast Asian nations attempt to manage significant migration flows. The meetings with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim represent a rare instance of high-level diplomatic engagement for the junta leader, who has largely been isolated by regional blocs since seizing power in a 2021 military takeover.
The central focus of the bilateral discussions is the systematic return of undocumented Myanmar migrants currently detained in Malaysian immigration facilities. While the Malaysian government frames the initiative as a necessary and voluntary resolution to a logistical burden, international human rights organisations have fiercely condemned the arrangement. Critics argue that returning individuals to a nation embroiled in active civil conflict exposes them to severe risks, including political persecution and forced military conscription under the junta’s increasingly stringent national service laws.
Diplomatic Engagement and Repatriation Plans
The logistical framework for the mass deportations is already operational. On September 29, Malaysia coordinated the return of nearly 1,500 Myanmar nationals via naval and hospital ships. According to official statements from Kuala Lumpur, this represents merely the initial phase of a broader agreement that will see approximately 5,000 individuals sent back to Myanmar. Malaysian authorities assert that these individuals, drawn from the roughly 11,800 Myanmar nationals held in domestic immigration detention depots as of late August, have agreed to be repatriated in stages.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has defended the policy as a pragmatic diplomatic effort aimed at securing a long-term solution to the country’s migration pressures. The Malaysian government maintains that it cannot host undocumented migrants indefinitely and insists that Myanmar must take responsibility for its citizens. During the parliamentary sessions leading up to the visit, Anwar emphasized that Malaysia would demand guarantees from the Myanmar government that returning citizens would face proper treatment, free from abuse or human rights violations upon arrival.
Human Rights Organisations Raise Alarms
The assurances of safe return have done little to placate the international community. Prominent advocacy groups, including Human Rights Watch and Fortify Rights, have demanded the immediate suspension of the deportations and urged the cancellation of Min Aung Hlaing’s visit. The organisations point to the volatile security situation across vast swathes of Myanmar, noting that the military government continues to conduct airstrikes and ground offensives against civilian populations and armed resistance groups, creating an inherently unsafe environment for any returnees.
A critical point of contention is the lack of independent oversight in the repatriation process. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) has expressed deep concern over the returns, highlighting that Malaysian authorities have not permitted the agency to conduct individual protection assessments. Without these independent evaluations, rights groups argue it is impossible to verify whether the deportations are truly voluntary or whether individuals with legitimate fears of persecution—who are entitled to international protection—are being forcibly returned to a conflict zone.
The Regional Refugee Situation
The repatriation efforts highlight the precarious status of refugees in Malaysia, a nation that is not a signatory to the 1951 UN Refugee Convention. Consequently, Malaysia does not legally differentiate between asylum seekers and undocumented economic migrants, leaving vulnerable populations exposed to arrest and detention. The country currently hosts over 215,000 refugees registered with the UNHCR, the majority of whom have fled the protracted crises in Myanmar seeking safety and economic stability.
Of particular concern is the fate of the Rohingya minority, who make up a substantial portion of the refugee population in Malaysia. The Rohingya have faced decades of systemic persecution and denial of citizenship in Myanmar, culminating in the 2017 military crackdowns that forced hundreds of thousands to flee. While Malaysian authorities have not specified the ethnic composition of the recent deportees, the prospect of returning Rohingya to the authority of the very military leaders who orchestrated their displacement has drawn intense international scrutiny and condemnation.
ASEAN's Ongoing Dilemma
Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Kuala Lumpur also spotlights the deep divisions within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) regarding how to handle the Myanmar crisis. Since the 2021 coup, ASEAN has barred the junta’s senior leadership from top-level summits, citing a failure to implement the agreed-upon Five-Point Consensus aimed at restoring peace. However, individual member states have increasingly pursued unilateral engagements based on their specific national interests.
The Malaysian Foreign Ministry has framed the bilateral meetings as an opportunity for Prime Minister Anwar to sustain direct engagement with Myanmar in a manner consistent with ASEAN’s goals. By maintaining diplomatic channels, Malaysia hopes to exert influence over the junta’s domestic policies and facilitate regional stability. Nevertheless, providing an official platform to a leader implicated in severe human rights abuses risks undermining ASEAN’s collective stance and granting the military regime the international legitimacy it desperately seeks amidst a grueling domestic conflict.

The former junta chief is on a two-day visit to Malaysia as he looks for greater international legitimacy after being appointed as president in April following an election that was widely criticised by Western nations and rights groups as a sham.
Myanmar has been in turmoil since Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup against a democratically elected government in 2021, triggering a nationwide civil war.

“I would say that we and our part in Malaysia, will do whatever is possible to make sure that we enhance this collaboration and ultimately, take Myanmar as part of our community of nations, without prejudice, and particularly in the context of ASEAN,” Anwar told a media briefing following the meeting.

articles.title: As South China Sea reefs die, states need to rise above debate - Lowy Institute
articles.summary: As South China Sea reefs die, states need to rise above debate  Lowy Institute
articles.full_text:
China Coast Guard vessels near Scarborough Shoal in the South China Sea (Wang Peng/Xinhua via Getty Images)
As South China Sea reefs die, states need to rise above debate
Ocean life does not oblige claims of sovereignty, so cooperation that transcends geopolitics is urgently needed for environmental protection.
On 15 August 2026, China published an ecological assessment of the South China Sea (Opens in new window) stating that the coral cover around Sandy Cay has declined by nearly 70% compared to 2016. The cause is said to be a combination of natural factors and extensive human activity. The report comes after months of China and the Philippines accusing each other of damage to coral reefs in the area – and can be seen as a way for China to blame the Philippines for the degradation of Sandy Cay.
The South China Sea is one of the most biodiverse (Opens in new window) marine areas in the Indo-Pacific, with a rich ecosystem of coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass meadows and fisheries. However, since China’s massive reclamation in 2013-2015, there have been changes in these ecosystems. Satellite imagery tracking by the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative (Opens in new window) indicates China has taken possession of more than 1,300 hectares of submerged coral reefs to build seven artificial islands in the Spratly Islands, including an air base at Fiery Cross Reef and a military port facility at Mischief Reef.
Sand dredging and landfill damage important habitats for marine life. Current-borne sedimentation pollutes surrounding waters, including unreclaimed areas. A 2016 arbitration (Opens in new window) award found that China breached its obligation to protect marine ecosystems, and it rejected the nine-dash line (Opens in new window), but China rejected (Opens in new window) the arbitration. In addition to China, Vietnam and the Philippines have expanded artificial land in their control areas, adding to the damage.
The first step is to strengthen the joint ecological survey mechanism between ASEAN and China, with the support of independent research institutions and, where necessary, international organisations.
In Savage Ecology: War and Geopolitics at the End of the World (Opens in new window), Jairus Victor Grove views contemporary geopolitical order as a condition shaped by war and political violence. For Grove, war is not just an instrument of policy, but rather a relationship between humans, technology, materiality, and the environment, with far-reaching ecological consequences. This perspective is illustrated in the South China Sea, where territorial competition, militarisation, resource extraction, and pressure on marine ecosystems go hand in hand.
This is the military logic behind the report. The living, connected sea, where larvae and fish stocks drift across every line on the map, are flattened into points to be dominated, each affixed to flags, ships, warplanes, and legal arguments. The ocean does not adhere to these clear delineations, but political claims require it.
What happens is the translation of ecological science into proof points. Coral reef monitoring data is produced for legal and diplomatic purposes, not to guide the co-management of degraded ecosystems. Distrust makes joint management a concession, so all parties produce one-sided evidence. States debate who is entitled to a reef, while the coral continues to lose its live cover.
Maxar satellite imagery of the 2014 dredging by China t Fiery Cross Reef in the South China Sea, a part of the Spratly Islands group (Maxar Technologies/Getty Images)
An alternative to this is environmental cooperation – an opportunity to rebuild the trust eroded by strategic competition. The first step is to strengthen the joint ecological survey mechanism between ASEAN and China, with the support of independent research institutions and, where necessary, international organisations. Learning from the Joint Marine Seismic Undertaking (JMSU) (Opens in new window)’s failures, this requires a transparent and standardised methodology, periodic monitoring, and a shared database on coral reef conditions, water quality, and fishery resources. Data and methodologies that are not security sensitive need to be made available and auditable by all participants. All activities should be under a without prejudice clause that affirms that participation, site access, data exchange, and use of research results do not diminish, recognise, or alter the legal position or sovereignty claims of any party.
In addition, the region needs marine science institutions with sustainable technical capacity designed to remain functional when political relations heat up, complete with clear technical mandates, stable funding, data verification procedures, and a no-prejudice clause. Their job is not to determine sovereignty, but rather to provide a transparent evidence base. These institutions become a separate technical layer from the dynamics of the dispute.
This is not an easy solution. Environmental protection needs to run parallel to dispute resolution. Claimants will need to agree that unresolved disputes should not be a reason to allow ecosystems to deteriorate.
The South China Sea issue also represents a broader challenge – how do countries deal with ecosystems that know no boundaries? Ecological reports and surveys should not just be used to strengthen positions, but as a warning that the space to delay action is getting narrower. If diplomacy fails to go beyond claims and counterclaims, scientific cooperation and environmental protection can be the starting point for rebuilding trust.

articles.title: [不同来源] [Big read] Can ASEAN continue to reap economic benefits from the US-China rivalry? - ThinkChina
articles.summary: [Big read] Can ASEAN continue to reap economic benefits from the US-China rivalry?  ThinkChina
articles.full_text:
Southeast Asia once benefited from China-US rivalry as companies shifted supply chains into the region. Now, tighter US rules are forcing countries to account for their Chinese links — and putting their strategic neutrality to the test. Lianhe Zaobao journalist Zhou Yifei finds out.
(Edited and refined by Grace Chong, with the assistance of AI translation.)
In June, Malaysian law enforcement authorities seized 72 servers at Kuala Lumpur International Airport that were being smuggled out of the country and contained advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips, with the shipment valued at around 52.9 million ringgit (US$12.5 million). Shortly before that, in February, Indonesia reached a reciprocal trade agreement with the US, making numerous concessions in sensitive areas including mutual recognition of standards, intellectual property protection, regulation of state-owned enterprises and export controls. Meanwhile, the US is stepping up scrutiny of Chinese goods being transshipped through Vietnam to circumvent tariffs and rules of origin.
These three seemingly unrelated events all point to the same structural shift: over the past decade, China-US rivalry has pushed large amounts of manufacturing capacity, foreign investment and trade orders towards Southeast Asia. Now, Southeast Asian countries increasingly have to prove to the US exactly whose components go into their exports, whose technology they use and even which Chinese rules their domestic industrial policies are aligning with.
Southeast Asia continues to go to great lengths to avoid “choosing sides”, but the cost of maintaining strategic neutrality and room for policy manoeuvre is becoming increasingly high.
Shrinking geopolitical dividends
Since the China-US trade war erupted in 2018, an increasing number of multinational companies have adopted a “China+1” strategy, extending the assembly, processing and export stages of production for European and American markets into Southeast Asia, while remaining heavily dependent on China for components, raw materials, production equipment and mature supplier networks.
Benefiting from this major industrial shift, Southeast Asia has become a key beneficiary of the restructuring of global supply chains. Between 2018 and 2025, Vietnam’s total exports to the US surged from US$49.1 billion to US$193.9 billion, almost quadrupling. Over the same period, Thailand’s total exports to the US also tripled.
With US President Donald Trump entering his second presidential term in 2025, great power rivalry has entered a new phase. The supply chain model of “Made in China, assembled in Southeast Asia, exported to Europe and the US” has not collapsed, but the rules of the game have fundamentally changed.
Le Hong Hiep, a senior fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, told Lianhe Zaobao that Washington threatened last July to impose punitive tariffs of 40% on Chinese goods deemed to have been transshipped through Vietnam. As the average effective US tariff on Chinese goods is currently about 41%, Vietnam still retains a significant cost advantage as a destination for relocated manufacturing.
The more serious challenge, however, is not tariffs, but the far-reaching rules underpinning them. Le pointed out, “The definitions of origin and transshipment remain unresolved, while Washington’s effort to limit Chinese content in goods produced elsewhere in Southeast Asia suggests a broader campaign against the ‘made in China, finished in Vietnam’ model.”
For multinational companies, more resilient supply chains are certainly needed, while Chinese companies are bound to continue expanding their investments in Southeast Asia. The geopolitical dividends generated by China-US rivalry have not disappeared entirely, but the threshold for accessing them has risen markedly. Southeast Asian countries now have to answer not only “Where was the product made?” but also clearly account for “Who invested, who supplied the components, and whose technology was used?”
US draws red lines
The escalation of China-US economic rivalry does not mean Southeast Asian countries will be split into two parallel economic blocs with zero interaction. Commercial realities show that the costs would be staggering if the US forcibly severed all Southeast Asian industries linked to Chinese supply chains. As a result, the prospect of a comprehensive decoupling in general consumer and civilian industries such as consumer electronics remains limited.
Robert Walker, a research fellow at the Lowy Institute’s Indo-Pacific Development Centre, said in an interview that the real concern is the selective fragmentation — and even partial decoupling — in strategically critical industries.
At the forefront are cutting-edge high-tech sectors such as semiconductors, data centres and AI, which are particularly vulnerable to the direct impact of the major powers’ expanding export controls, investment security reviews and rules of origin requirements.
Malaysia’s semiconductor industry is a case in point. The country accounts for about 13% of global semiconductor packaging and testing capacity. Its mature electronics industry, open investment environment and relatively neutral trade and economic position have attracted investment from multinational companies such as Intel.
Now, as the US calls on its allies and partners to tighten controls on the flow of advanced chips to China, Malaysia can no longer simply serve as a neutral processing and transshipment hub. It is instead being forced to take on stringent supply chain compliance requirements and scrutiny over the destination of its products.
Last July, the Malaysian government announced that exports, transshipments and transits of all US-origin high-performance AI chips would require prior approval from the country’s trade regulator. Malaysian authorities have also begun investigating several cases involving the suspected illegal transshipment of controlled advanced chips and servers, signalling their determination to meet compliance obligations.
Critical minerals another pressure point
Critical minerals are another high-stakes battleground. As the world’s largest nickel producer, Indonesia’s nickel mining industry is deeply bound to Chinese capital, with Chinese companies controlling about three-quarters of the country’s nickel refining capacity.
This puts Indonesia at the crossroads of the China-US contest over critical minerals. The reciprocal trade agreement signed by the US and Indonesia in February this year also covers the minerals sector. Among other provisions, it requires foreign-invested mineral processing facilities to comply with Indonesian mining quotas and strictly limits production above those quotas. The two sides also agreed to strengthen export controls and investment security cooperation involving relevant critical minerals.
Walker pointed out that semiconductor and critical mineral supply chains are highly concentrated, making them more susceptible to being used as instruments of pressure by major powers. “Countries and economies can therefore be more easily excluded from their use, which can be particularly painful, making it both an intolerable vulnerability and a tempting point of geopolitical leverage.”
These two sectors are also important inputs for dual-use technologies, used in both civilian and military contexts. Walker stressed that once military capabilities are involved, geopolitical considerations will naturally take precedence over commercial logic.
Trade policy expands into economic security
Of greater concern to Southeast Asian countries is that US trade policy is expanding beyond tariff negotiations into a comprehensive set of economic security rules.
Although the reciprocal trade agreement between Indonesia and the US reduced the reciprocal tariff from 32% to 19%, the concessions sought by Washington in return go far beyond tariff reductions.
Arianto Patunru, a fellow at the Crawford School of Public Policy at the Australian National University, said in an interview that the agreement reflects a broader shift in US trade policy: market access is no longer unconditional, but is increasingly linked to regulatory, industrial and economic security commitments.
Under the agreement, he noted, Indonesia is required to adjust its domestic legal framework in areas including product content requirements, the issuance of import licences, investment rules, digital trade, intellectual property protection, labour standards and environmental protection. It must also closely coordinate with the US on export controls, investment security reviews and measures to prevent transshipment.
The agreement even extends to economic and national security, as well as Indonesia’s economic and trade relations with third countries. Indonesia must align its export controls with those of the US on sensitive technologies and critical goods, and ensure that Indonesian companies do not fill market gaps created by US restrictions. If Indonesia subsequently signs a new bilateral free trade agreement or preferential economic agreement with a country that “jeopardises essential US interests”, Washington may reassess the US-Indonesia agreement. If consultations fail, it could even terminate the agreement and restore the original reciprocal tariff.
Shrinking strategic autonomy
Some argue that the reciprocal trade agreement could help push Indonesia to address the problems of policy inconsistency and regulatory instability, ultimately benefiting businesses, consumers and the country’s overall competitiveness. Others, however, are concerned that reforms driven under intense external tariff pressure could constrain Indonesia’s room for strategic autonomy as a sovereign state.

articles.title: South China Sea talks highlight communication and UNCLOS adherence to prevent escalation - Asia News Network
articles.summary: South China Sea talks highlight communication and UNCLOS adherence to prevent escalation  Asia News Network
articles.full_text:
HANOI – Greater communication, transparency, restraint and adherence to international law are essential to preventing misunderstandings at sea from escalating into incidents and, ultimately, crises, heard at 18th South China Sea International Conference in Hà Nội on Wednesday.
The message emerged as a common thread among the remarks of host and guests at the two-day convention, themed “Contestation, Connectivity, and Cooperation: The South China Sea and the Regional Maritime Order” this year, which brings together policymakers, diplomats, military representatives and scholars from Việt Nam, ASEAN, and countries beyond the region.
Experts and diplomats converged on one concern: as the South China Sea (known in Việt Nam as the East Sea) becomes increasingly crowded, technologically sophisticated and strategically contested, the margin for miscalculation is narrowing.
Dr. Nguyễn Hùng Sơn, president of the Diplomatic Academy of Việt Nam, said the conference had, over nearly two decades, sought to provide a forum where parties with different perspectives could listen to one another, exchange ideas and build trust.
He framed the East Sea not merely as a collection of territorial disputes, but as a shared concern involving peace, stability, international law and the global commons.
This approach is becoming increasingly important as maritime security itself changes, he said. Disruptions to major sea routes can rapidly affect energy supplies, shipping costs and livelihoods, while climate change, pollution and pressure on marine resources are adding new challenges.
At the same time, automation, artificial intelligence and undersea cables are transforming ports, logistics and maritime operations.
“The deeper our connectivity becomes, the more disruption in one place can create vulnerability elsewhere,” Sơn said in his opening remarks.
He identified the central challenge as finding ways to manage contestation while protecting the connectivity that underpins regional prosperity and creating more room for cooperation.
The conference, he said, should ask how contestation can be managed, how connectivity can be protected, how cooperation can be broadened even amid uncertainty, and ultimately how the East Sea can become “not a fault line of regional division” but a foundation for an inclusive regional maritime order.
Preventing incidents before they become crises
Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Nguyễn Thị Hoàng Vân placed the problem in a broader regional and global context, noting that the intersection of security, economics, technology and geopolitics is making the maritime domain simultaneously more important and more vulnerable.
The East Sea reflects these wider trends, she said, with a denser operational presence, expanding capabilities, new technologies and continuing close-range encounters creating a more crowded and less predictable environment.
The result is a potentially shorter distance between an incident and a crisis.
For Việt Nam, the answer is not to assume that strategic differences can be eliminated, but to develop mechanisms capable of managing them.
“Not every dispute can be resolved immediately, but many risks can be managed now,” she said.
Communication, transparency and practical confidence-building measures can prevent misunderstandings from becoming incidents and incidents from becoming crises, she argued.
For Việt Nam, international law – particularly the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) – provides the foundation for such predictability.
Vân stressed that rules matter most when reflected in actual behaviour. Rights must be accompanied by responsibilities, she said, while differences should be managed in ways that reduce misunderstanding and prevent escalation.
She also pointed to the ASEAN–China Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the East Sea and negotiations towards an effective and substantive Code of Conduct as mechanisms that can contribute to confidence-building and risk reduction.
But cooperation should not be limited to dispute management, and must be extended towards practical areas such as maritime safety, environmental protection, sustainable use of marine resources and the resilience of critical maritime infrastructure, which can help build up trusts.
Philippine Undersecretary of Foreign Affairs Leo M. Herrera-Lim, who is also an ASEAN Philippines Senior Officials’ Meeting (SOM) Leader while the Philippines holds the ASEAN Chairmanship this year, highlighted the rule of law, arguing that contestation, connectivity and cooperation must be anchored in predictable rules.
For the Philippines, UNCLOS and the 2016 South China Sea Arbitral Award remain key reference points.
The Philippines and Việt Nam, he said, have developed mechanisms for preventing and managing incidents, including their joint working group on maritime and oceans concerns, a 2024 memorandum of understanding on incident prevention and management in the East Sea, and growing cooperation between their coast guards.
Hotlines, reciprocal port visits, officer exchanges, marine scientific research and environmental cooperation demonstrate how mechanisms can translate diplomatic commitments into practical safeguards.
Herrera-Lim also cited instances in which Vietnamese and Philippine maritime personnel had assisted sailors and fishermen in distress, describing such actions as evidence of solidarity that transcends political differences.
Communication must exist before the crisis
Lieutenant-General Derek A. Macaulay, Canada’s Senior Military Representative to the Indo-Pacific, said many maritime incidents do not begin with an intentional decision to escalate.
Instead, they can start with two crews operating in close proximity, uncertain about each other’s intentions and facing only a limited window in which to make the correct decision – which necessitates communication efforts.
“Communication channels must exist before a crisis because they cannot be improvised in the middle of one,” he said, against the backdrops of the increasing number and variety of vessels operating in regional waters. Navies, coast guards, fishing fleets, research vessels, commercial shipping and uncrewed systems are operating in a progressively complex maritime environment.
Keeping communication open even when governments disagree should be considered part of the professional responsibility of military forces, the Canadian official noted, adding that Canada’s own approach is to maintain a long-term regional presence while supporting dialogue, diplomacy and ASEAN-centred mechanisms rather than confrontation.
Transparency as a tool for crisis prevention
Australia’s Deputy Secretary of Foreign Affairs and Trade Michelle Chan similarly held that international law is particularly important in an environment where power is unequal because it protects the rights of states regardless of their size.
She stressed that responsible maritime conduct means respecting the lawful rights of others and ensuring that competition does not escalate into conflict, and one practical measure is timely two-way information sharing on maritime incidents and developments.
Countries need an accurate picture of what is happening at sea if they are to exercise their rights, protect their interests and respond in ways that reduce rather than increase escalation risks, she said.
Greater transparency can reduce uncertainty, strengthen maritime domain awareness and enable governments to make better-informed decisions.
The point is significant because miscalculation can arise not only from hostile intent, but from incomplete or inaccurate information about another actor’s intentions, and in that sense, transparency becomes a form of preventive security, according to the Australian official.
Chan also highlighted the role of ASEAN-led institutions in bringing regional countries and major powers together, building habits of dialogue and reinforcing expectations of responsible conduct.
Australia is supporting maritime security and legal-capacity building, information sharing, training and marine science cooperation with regional partners, including Việt Nam.

articles.summary: Leading Furniture Exporters: China Dominates the Market  وردنا
articles.full_text:
The global furniture market is witnessing fierce competition among producing nations. It is no longer just about the size of factories; production costs, material quality, delivery speed, design, and the ability to meet global market demands are crucial factors.
China leads this arena by a large margin, successfully establishing an expansive industrial sector that covers all types of home, office, and outdoor furniture.
Which Country Leads Furniture Exports Globally?
China tops the list of global furniture exporters, significantly outpacing most competitors. Reports from the furniture market indicate that China holds a substantial share of the international furniture trade, with exports valued at tens of billions of dollars annually.
China's strength lies in its vast industrial base, capable of producing large quantities at competitive costs. Its advanced infrastructure, ports, transport networks, and local supply chains enhance its ability to serve importers worldwide.
Why Does China Lead in Furniture Exports?
China's strength in this sector relies on several intertwined factors, including a massive manufacturing base, availability of materials and components, and logistics services near factories. The country also has extensive experience manufacturing furniture for export markets.
Guangdong's Foshan City stands out as a key industrial and commercial hub for the furniture industry, housing numerous companies, factories, and specialized exhibitions, making it a vital global furniture trade destination.
Vietnam: A Strong Asian Competitor
Vietnam holds a prominent position in the global furniture trade, particularly in wooden furniture. The Vietnamese furniture industry has significantly expanded in recent years, driven by increased demand from American and European markets.
Vietnam benefits from its Asian location and proximity to regional supply chains, supported by foreign investments in manufacturing. Vietnamese companies have also capitalized on shifts in global trade, such as redistributing some manufacturing processes away from China.
Wooden furniture is a critical strength for Vietnam, with exports of tables, chairs, bedroom sets, and outdoor furniture reaching global markets.
Poland: A European Furniture Powerhouse
Poland is a leading European nation in furniture manufacturing and exporting, becoming a key industrial center serving many markets within and outside the European Union.
The Polish industry is known for producing flat-pack furniture as well as home and office furniture. Poland's geographic location, close to European markets, reduces transport costs and enhances its competitive advantage.
Poland is also integrated into supply chains of major global furniture companies, with notable names like IKEA relying on an extensive network of suppliers and manufacturers in the region.
Germany: Quality and Engineering in Furniture Manufacturing
Germany maintains an advanced position in the global furniture market, emphasizing quality, precise engineering, and practical design.
The German industry is particularly renowned for office furniture, fitted kitchens, and high-quality furniture, relying on advanced production techniques and durable materials.
Germany does not necessarily compete on low prices but focuses on quality, added value, technology, and design, making its products desirable in markets seeking long-lasting, high-spec furniture.
Italy: The Capital of Design and Luxury Furniture
Italy holds a distinguished position among furniture-exporting countries, with its strength particularly tied to design, innovation, and luxury furniture.
Italy is globally renowned for designing elegant furniture pieces, hosting numerous brands and designers influencing global interior decor trends. The Milan Furniture Fair is a major international event gathering companies, designers, and buyers from across markets.
Italian products have a competitive edge distinct from low-cost goods, focusing on design, materials, finishes, and craftsmanship, asserting their presence in the luxury furniture sector.
Ranking of Leading Furniture Exporting Countries
While exact rankings depend on the year and statistical definitions used, the list of major exporters usually includes the following industrial giants:
Key Players in Global Furniture Trade
1. China: Dominates through massive manufacturing size, low production costs, and integrated supply chains.
2. Vietnam: A growing force in wooden furniture, with a broad presence in American and European markets.
3. Poland: A key furniture manufacturing center in Europe with a strong supply network within the EU.
4. Germany: Relying on quality, advanced engineering, and high-spec office furniture and kitchens.
5. Italy: Known for luxury furniture, design, innovation, and upscale brands.
Other significant producers and exporters include the United States, Turkey, Canada, Mexico, and some European and Asian countries, varying based on the year of statistics and trade classifications.
Turkey: A Prominent Player in the Regional Furniture Market
In recent years, Turkey has emerged as one of the leading furniture-exporting nations, particularly in the Middle East. Turkey's industry has benefited from its strategic location between Europe, Asia, and the Middle East and diverse, competitively priced products.
Turkish products reach many markets, including Iraq, Saudi Arabia, the Gulf states, and Europe. Turkish companies have a strong presence across bedroom, living room, kitchen, and office furniture sectors.
Turkey's competitive edge lies in combining modern design, mid-range prices, acceptable quality, and quick access to nearby markets, helping increase its exports and international presence.
Why Does China Dominate the Global Furniture Market?
China’s dominance is attributed to various industrial and economic advantages, most significantly, its enormous manufacturing base capable of producing millions of pieces with varying specifications and prices.
China also has a broad network of wood suppliers, industrial materials, accessories, and components, reducing time and costs for final product manufacturing.
Key Strengths of China’s Furniture Industry
- Extensive production capacity.
- Low manufacturing costs in multiple sectors.
- A broad network of material and component suppliers.
- Strong infrastructure and ports.
- Easy access to global markets.
- Diverse products and price ranges.
- Ability to manufacture products according to importers’ specifications.
- Proliferation of specialized industrial cities and areas.
What Are the Most Exported Furniture Types Globally?
The international furniture trade is diverse and includes not only bedroom and living room furniture but also office furniture, kitchens, outdoor furniture, seating, tables, and cabinets.
Home Furniture
Includes bedroom sets, living rooms, tables, chairs, cabinets, and other home products.
Office Furniture
Includes desks, chairs, cabinets, and storage systems, witnessing continuous demand as businesses and commercial spaces expand.
Garden and Outdoor Furniture
Includes chairs, tables, and couches for outdoor use, increasingly demanded in markets with suitable climates and open spaces.
Is China the World's Largest Furniture Manufacturer or Exporter?
There is a distinction between furniture production and export. A country may be a major producer but consume a significant portion of its output locally, while others focus more on exporting.
China enjoys a significant advantage in both, combining a massive manufacturing base with a large domestic market and an extensive exporting sector serving global markets.
This dual capacity means assessing the strength of a furniture industry involves not only export value but also production size, domestic market size, added value, number of factories, and global trade share.
Is Chinese Furniture Better Than European Furniture?
Furniture quality should not be determined solely by the country of origin. China produces furniture at various quality levels and prices, ranging from budget to high-specifications products.
In contrast, countries like Germany and Italy are known for providing high value-added products in specific sectors, particularly luxury furniture, design, and engineering. Therefore, furniture choice depends on budget, materials, design, manufacturing quality, and intended use, not just the country of origin.
The Future of Global Furniture Trade
The global furniture sector is moving towards more changes due to rising shipping costs, shifting supply chains, and increasing emphasis on sustainability and eco-friendly materials. E-commerce has become crucial for manufacturers to reach consumers and importers in new markets.
Simultaneously, demand is growing for recyclable furniture, responsibly sourced wood products, and smart, flexible furniture suitable for small spaces.
While China is likely to continue playing a major role in the global market, countries like Vietnam, Turkey, and Poland are trying to expand their export share through investment in manufacturing, design, and supply chains.
In conclusion, China leads the list of top furniture exporting countries worldwide by a substantial margin, benefiting from a massive industrial base, integrated supply chains, and a great ability to produce various furniture types at competitive prices.
With the ongoing changes in global trade dynamics, competition in the furniture sector now relies on a mix of price, quality, design, and delivery speed, not just production volume alone.

articles.summary: Indonesia, EU push to conclude trade deal by end-October  Indonesia Business Post
articles.full_text:
Jakarta seeks to accelerate ratification of the I-EU CEPA so the agreement can take effect in early 2027 and preserve preferential access to the European market.
Indonesia is pushing to sign the Indonesia-European Union Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (I-EU CEPA) by the end of October 2026, as Jakarta seeks to avoid disruption when the European Union’s Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP) facility ends in 2027.
Trade Minister Budi Santoso said the government aims to accelerate the agreement’s ratification after signing so it can enter into force in January 2027.
“That is why we are pushing for it to be signed at the end of October,” Santoso said on Tuesday.
The government has held discussions with EU member-state ambassadors, led by Coordinating Minister for Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto, and both sides have agreed to target completion of the signing by the end of October, potentially in Jakarta.
Several technical matters are still being finalised, including the language of the agreement. Indonesia wants the final document to be issued in both Indonesian and English.
Securing market access
Santoso said completing the agreement on schedule is important because the EU’s GSP currently provides tariff preferences for certain Indonesian exports. Without the facility, those tariff preferences would no longer apply.
The I-EU CEPA negotiations took about 10 years to complete. Once implemented, the agreement is expected to provide zero-percent tariffs for many Indonesian export products and improve market access for commodities including sustainable palm oil and its derivatives, footwear, textiles and fishery products.
Airlangga said the legal drafting of the agreement in English is nearing completion before the document is submitted for consideration by the European Parliament and subsequently goes through Indonesia’s ratification process.
He said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is scheduled to visit Indonesia in late October or early November, while EU Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maroš Šefčovič is also expected to visit as discussions on the agreement move toward completion.
The government expects the CEPA to strengthen market access, trade and business engagement between Indonesia and the EU, while supporting higher trade and investment flows.

JOHOR BAHRU – All schools in Johor will be closed on Oct 8 and 9 due to the worsening haze and deteriorating air quality across the state.
Johor education and information committee chairman Muhammad Naqib Md Ghazali said the decision was made following the directive of Johor Regent Tunku Ismail Sultan Ibrahim as a precautionary measure to safeguard the health and safety of students.
The Panti assemblyman added that the state government understood that the closure could affect parents and guardians who still had to work.
“Therefore, the cooperation and consideration of employers is greatly appreciated in providing appropriate flexibility to affected parents, including reasonable work arrangements according to the suitability of their respective organisations,” he said in a statement on Oct 7.
Muhammad Naqib said schools involved in the Year Four Learning Matrix (MPT4) or any other assessments would postpone the exercises.
“The assessments will be rescheduled subject to the decisions of the Johor Education Department and relevant parties,” he said.
He added that home-based teaching and learning (PdPR) would be conducted during the two-day closure to ensure students could continue their lessons.

Malaysia’s state education departments, district education offices and educational institutions under the Education Ministry have been told to take immediate steps if the haze worsens in their area.
The ministry said in a statement on Oct 7 that schools should implement the preventive measures listed in past circulars regarding preparations for hot and dry weather, as well as steps for areas critically affected by haze.
