Acknowledging that the haze had caused API readings in several locations to reach unhealthy levels, the ministry said the state departments, district offices and educational institutions should obtain the latest air quality status via the Department of Environment’s website.

Existential AI Threats and Bubble Fears Shape Singapore Finance Forums
AI Risks and Market Sentiment at Singapore Finance Conferences
By Ankur Banerjee
AI Risks Take Center Stage
SINGAPORE, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Existential and financial risks posed by the artificial intelligence boom were top of mind for investors and policymakers at two conferences in Singapore on Wednesday, highlighting a cautious shift in mood around the AI trade.
Concerns that once centred on frothy valuations have broadened into a wide swathe of fears, including autonomous systems slipping out of human control, AI-designed bioweapons and the possibility that massive spending on the technology may never pay off.
Loss of Control and Bioweapon Fears
"Anyone who tells you I've got absolute control over my autonomous agent... obviously doesn't know what he's talking about. So loss of control is a real threat," Singaporean Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan said at the Milken Institute Asia Summit.
Last month, the heads of leading US AI labs came together in a rare show of unity to call for slowing the technology's development, warning it could soon improve on its own and slip beyond human control.
Claude maker Anthropic plans to caution potential investors in its IPO that advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Reuters reported last week.
State and Non-State Threats
Balakrishnan said on Wednesday the risk of state and non-state actors using the technology to build new weapons, "whether it's in chemistry or biology or in weapons of mass destruction, is very real."
Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, founder and chairperson of Indian biopharmaceutical firm Biocon, said that while AI was a force for good, bad actors could use it to design new viruses or pathogens.
"The real existential threat is bioterrorism," she said at the Forbes Global CEO Conference, calling for guardrails and governance. "I don't think self-governance is going to work."
Bubble Worries and Market Impact
BUBBLE WORRIES LINGER
Investors' faith in the AI trade has propped up the stock market even as higher energy prices and episodic routs in the bond market have pushed borrowing costs in major economies to multi-decade highs.
But worries over how long the AI rally can last and what it means for global markets have persist.
Market Risks and Investor Sentiment
"If the AI narrative is unwound because of safety issues, regulation or because as we go through 2027, end users don't see sufficient ROI (return on investment), there could be issues," said Rohit Sipahimalani, chief investment officer at Singapore state investor Temasek.
"The biggest risk to the market is the AI narrative. Right now, it seems very strong," Sipahimalani said at the Milken Institute event.
Bubble Dynamics and Rate Pressures
Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio was less sanguine, saying AI was in a "classic bubble" and there was a difference between "how terrific a technology is and how terrific an investment is."
He told the Forbes event that rising rates and changing circumstances had not "yet had a negative effect on other things," but that there was pressure for interest rates to rise further.
Once higher rates began to bite, the bubble would start to burst, Dalio said. "I think we're close to that."
(Reporting by Ankur Banerjee, Tom Westbrook and Xinghui Kok in Singapore, editing by Xevi Fontdegloria)

articles.title: Vietnam targets low-altitude economy making up 1.5% of GDP by 2045 - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Vietnam targets low-altitude economy making up 1.5% of GDP by 2045  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Vietnam aims to turn its nascent low-altitude airspace into a new economic and technological growth engine, with the sector targeted to contribute about 1.5% of national GDP by 2045, under a new policy conclusion by Politburo, the country's highest decision-making body.
The Politburo's Conclusion 99-KL/TW, issued on September 28, identifies low-altitude airspace as a national resource, a new space for economic development, and a special domain of national sovereignty. The policy seeks to develop strategic technologies while strengthening governance, national defense, security, and safety.
The move marks a shift from viewing low-altitude airspace primarily as an area for managing aircraft and flight activities toward developing an economic ecosystem covering aviation technologies, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), data, infrastructure, and related services.
By 2030, Vietnam aims to have three national-level flight testing zones in operation across different geographical conditions, as well as at least one national research and testing center for UAVs.
By 2045, the low-altitude economy is expected to become an important economic and technical sector, with strong regional competitiveness and a contribution of about 1.5% of GDP. Vietnam also aims to raise the domestic content ratio of key UAV models used in production to more than 30-40% by 2030 and above 85% by 2045.
The Ministry of Science and Technology (MoST) said the targets go beyond expanding the market for UAV applications. They are intended to support technological self-reliance, build domestic industrial capacity, and gradually establish local supply chains.
The policy also links the development of low-altitude airspace with national capabilities in technology, critical infrastructure, and strategic data, creating opportunities for domestic companies to participate more deeply in emerging technology value chains.
State to lead early market development
The government will play a leading role in establishing the initial market through public procurement, pilot programs and the use of UAVs in public-sector applications, while encouraging companies, research institutes and universities to participate in research, development, manufacturing and commercialization.
Under the policy framework, the state will focus on developing legislation and governance systems, technical standards, essential infrastructure and an initial market. Businesses will serve as the main force in research, development, manufacturing, and commercialization of products and services.
Low-altitude airspace is expected to support a wide range of applications, with priority given to logistics, agriculture, natural-resource management, environmental protection, infrastructure monitoring, disaster prevention, search and rescue, emergency medical services and smart cities.
Creating an initial public-sector market could give domestic UAV companies an opportunity to develop technologies, improve production capabilities, and reduce costs before expanding into broader commercial markets.
The policy also calls for stronger coordination between central and local authorities, defense and security forces, and other relevant bodies to ensure unified and effective management of low-altitude activities.
Balance innovation with risk management
For an emerging technology sector, waiting until regulations are fully developed before allowing new applications could cause Vietnam to miss development opportunities, MoST noted. But opening the market too quickly without adequate safeguards could create risks involving safety, national defence, security, data and people's lawful rights and interests.
Conclusion 99 therefore calls for a unified and modern national governance model based on data, digital platforms, and risk management.
Activities in low-altitude airspace are to be managed according to operating areas, altitude levels, types of activity and risk levels. Management is also expected to cover the full operational cycle, from registration and identification to licensing, operation, monitoring, inspection, and enforcement.
The policy also calls for controlled testing, or sandbox mechanisms, for new technologies, products, services, and business models. Such programs would need clearly defined operating boundaries, time limits, evaluation criteria, monitoring mechanisms, and conditions for termination or expansion. The approach is designed to create room for innovation while maintaining national sovereignty, defense, security, and safety.
A sandbox, in this context, does not mean weaker regulation. Instead, it allows new technologies and business models to be tested within defined parameters and for a limited period. Authorities can then assess their effectiveness, identify risks, and refine regulations before considering wider deployment, the ministry noted.
The policy also calls for Vietnam to develop national technical standards and regulations, strengthen testing, inspection and certification capacity and gradually participate in international mechanisms and initiatives related to low-altitude airspace governance.
According to the MoST, Vietnam's low-altitude economy is forecast to record an annual growth rate of 13% to reach $500 million by 2035.

articles.title: MAS Sets New AI Risk Guidelines for Financial Institutions - Fintech Singapore
articles.summary: MAS Sets New AI Risk Guidelines for Financial Institutions  Fintech Singapore
articles.full_text:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has issued its finalised Guidelines on AI Risk Management for financial institutions.
Following a public consultation in November 2025, the framework sets out expectations for firms to manage risks across the AI lifecycle and address risks associated with third-party providers.
Under the guidelines, institutions can tailor their approach based on the scale and risk profile of their AI use.
Firms may also use existing governance structures to oversee these risks and do not need to establish dedicated AI committees.
MAS expects financial institutions to maintain inventories of their AI use and apply controls covering areas such as data governance, cybersecurity, testing, human oversight, monitoring and change management.
Institutions remain accountable for AI used in the services they deliver, including systems developed, operated or provided by third parties.
They should obtain sufficient assurance from providers and assess whether third-party AI is suitable for its intended use. Firms should also apply compensating controls where assurance gaps or practical constraints arise.
Where risks cannot be brought within an institution’s risk appetite, MAS said firms should consider limiting, suspending or replacing the third-party AI service.
Implementation will take place in phases. Sections 3 and 4 will take effect on 7 October 2027, while Sections 5 and 6 will apply from 7 October 2028.
MAS also highlighted the growing use of agentic AI systems that can operate autonomously and access tools.
In 2027, the regulator intends to consult the financial sector on what additional guidance for agentic AI would be useful.
“Realising these benefits sustainably requires financial institutions to understand and manage the risks that come with increasingly capable AI systems,”
said Ho Hern Shin, Deputy Managing Director at MAS.
She added that greater regulatory clarity will allow firms to innovate with confidence. It will also help maintain customer trust and the resilience of Singapore’s financial system.

From November 18 to 20, 2026, the Singapore FinTech Festival, organized by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the GFTN network, brings together central bankers, regulators, and digital asset players at Singapore EXPO. Piero Cipollone, who leads the digital euro at the European Central Bank, and the chairman of the supervisory board of Qivalis, the euro stablecoin of European banks, are among the speakers. Cointribune details what the program offers for crypto, what interests a European reader, and the cost of the pass.
To benefit from the Singapore FinTech Festival x Cointribune partnership discount (20% with code SMP-DISC-20-COINTRIBUNE), click here.
What is the Singapore FinTech Festival?
It is one of the largest global digital finance events, organized by the central bank of Singapore itself. The 2025 edition, the tenth, gathered more than 70,000 participants from 142 countries and territories and over 900 speakers, according to the report published by the organizers. MAS had announced trials of tokenized bonds settled in central bank money, as we reported in our article on Singapore’s tokenized bonds.
The 2026 edition is organized by MAS and the Global Finance & Technology Network (GFTN), together with the Association of Banks in Singapore, according to their press release of August 26, 2026. The festival is like a car show where you’d also meet the traffic code authors: companies and regulators exhibit side by side. Seen as an operation, it serves Singapore to position itself as a hub for digital finance; for the visitor, it costs a pass and a trip but gives access to central bankers rarely gathered in one place.
What place does crypto have in the program?
The 2026 theme, “The Coming Rewiring of the Financial System“, is divided into five sub-themes. Several directly relate to digital assets, according to the official themes page: the “tokenization chain”, corporate treasurers choosing their settlement asset among “deposits in dollars, local currencies, or stablecoins“, and the rules on digital assets beginning to apply on early markets.
Tokenization consists of representing an asset, such as a bond or a fund share, as a token on a blockchain. To understand this mechanism, read our explanation of tokenization. The head of GFTN already summarized the challenge at the previous edition:
The coming decade will be dedicated to responsibly harnessing AI, developing tokenization securely, and preparing for a quantum future.
Sopnendu Mohanty, Group CEO of GFTN, press release of November 9, 2025 (Cointribune translation)

|---|---|---|
| Piero Cipollone | Member of the ECB Executive Board | Chairs the Eurosystem working group on the digital euro |

The detailed session program is published over the weeks. The crypto sessions of previous editions, with Circle or Coinbase, were not yet confirmed for 2026 as of September 30.
What does this change for a European reader?
The festival offers a showcase for the European debate on digital currency. On the public side, the ECB is preparing the digital euro, a central bank digital currency; on the private side, 37 European banks, including BNP Paribas, BPCE, and Crédit Mutuel, are preparing with Qivalis a euro stablecoin, pending approval from DNB, according to the Qivalis website. The chairman of Qivalis’s supervisory board and a regulator examining its file will be on the same panel.
The ECB does not see the two projects as incompatible. On April 1, 2026, Piero Cipollone stated that “private settlement assets will play a role“, including “stablecoins denominated in euro issued in Europe“, according to the text of his speech (Cointribune translation). For a saver, the difference remains clear: the digital euro would be issued by the ECB, a stablecoin by a private company, whose solidity depends on its reserves.
How much does the pass cost?

articles.title: IMF chief warns of debt, energy and AI risks before Bangkok talks - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: IMF chief warns of debt, energy and AI risks before Bangkok talks  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
The global economy faces a difficult combination of record public debt, persistently high energy costs and both the opportunities and risks created by artificial intelligence, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned ahead of next week’s IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok.
Georgieva delivered her 2026 Annual Meetings Curtain Raiser speech in Singapore on Wednesday (October 7), setting out the main economic issues expected to confront finance ministers and central bank governors when they gather in Thailand from October 12–18.
Georgieva highlighted the rapid rise of the Asia-Pacific region since Thailand last hosted the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in 1991.
The region’s share of global GDP has increased from about 25% to 43%, underscoring Asia’s growing importance to global growth, trade and financial stability.
Against that backdrop, she identified three major forces shaping the global outlook: the rapid expansion of AI, prolonged high energy prices and mounting public debt.
“The global economy is being pulled in two opposite directions,” Georgieva said, describing a negative energy supply shock alongside a positive demand shock from AI.
Wars in Ukraine and the Gulf are adding to economic damage, particularly for countries heavily dependent on imported energy, while the AI investment boom is providing a new source of demand and economic activity.
AI is becoming an increasingly important driver of investment and trade.
Georgieva said investment in AI as a share of global GDP could eventually exceed the relative scale of previous infrastructure booms involving railways, electricity grids and telecommunications networks.
AI hardware and related technology products already account for more than 10% of world goods trade, with the United States, China and India among the major net importers as they build AI infrastructure.
Of the other seven economies among the world’s top 10 players in AI-related trade, five are Asian suppliers, highlighting the region’s strong position in technology supply chains.
However, Georgieva warned that the benefits are highly concentrated and could widen inequality if many countries are unable to gain access to the technology and the infrastructure needed to use it.
AI also brings financial risks. Heavy investment has increased pressure on technology companies to deliver the productivity and earnings expected by markets, meaning disappointment could trigger wider financial shocks.
Despite those risks, IMF research suggests that AI, if managed effectively, could add around 0.5 percentage point to annual global growth — an increase that Georgieva compared with adding an economy roughly the size of ASEAN to the world economy over time.
The AI boom is also increasing demand for electricity and other energy resources at a time when global fuel supplies remain under pressure.
Georgieva said crude oil prices remained around US$100 a barrel, while constraints on global refining capacity had added roughly another US$100 a barrel in refining margins for important products including diesel, pushing some refined fuel prices to record levels.
Liquefied natural gas supplies have also been disrupted by risks to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, with Asia and Europe particularly exposed.
Food, fertiliser and industrial input costs are also under pressure, while adverse weather poses an additional threat to food security.
With the Northern Hemisphere heading towards its colder months and countries expected to rebuild energy stocks, Georgieva borrowed a line from Game of Thrones: “Winter is coming.”
She warned that high energy prices could persist even if the Gulf conflict eased, with oil futures pointing to elevated prices through 2027.
Higher energy costs are feeding into inflation, policy interest rates and government borrowing costs.
Georgieva noted that 10-year sovereign bond yields in the United States, Germany and Japan had risen to their highest levels since 2007, 2009 and 1996, respectively.
Meanwhile, global public debt is approaching levels not seen since the aftermath of the Second World War and is projected to exceed 100% of global GDP before 2030.
Advanced economies carry some of the largest debt burdens, while emerging markets and low-income countries face their own difficulties as borrowing costs rise relative to revenue and economic growth.
Georgieva warned that governments could no longer rely solely on faster economic growth to bring debt ratios down, particularly after years in which interest rates were generally lower than economic growth rates.
She called for credible medium-term fiscal consolidation, particularly in highly indebted advanced economies, while stressing that governments should explain why fiscal adjustment is necessary, minimise damage to future growth and protect vulnerable groups.
Her message to policymakers gathering in Bangkok was clear: “We cannot keep delaying necessary policy action — you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them.”
Georgieva also said many central banks may need to maintain a “prudently hawkish bias”, with inflationary pressures coming not only from energy and food but also from the AI investment boom, tariffs, defence spending and high public debt.
She described recent rate increases by the US Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan as appropriate responses to persistent inflation risks.
At the same time, she warned that financial regulators need to closely monitor the AI-driven market boom, as high valuations and growing leverage could amplify any disappointment in technology-company earnings.
Georgieva said fiscal restraint and monetary policy alone would not be enough to address the world’s longer-term economic challenges.
Governments should also pursue reforms aimed at improving workforce skills, increasing labour-market flexibility, making it easier for businesses to enter and leave markets, expanding access to long-term capital, strengthening energy security and reducing unnecessary bureaucracy and outdated regulation.
International cooperation will also be essential if the benefits of AI are to spread beyond the economies currently leading the technology boom.
“In our interconnected world, countries cooperate not out of charity but out of self-interest,” Georgieva said.
The issues raised in Singapore are expected to form part of the wider debate when policymakers from the IMF’s member countries gather in Bangkok next week to discuss the global outlook, financial stability and policies for sustaining growth amid rising geopolitical, technological and fiscal pressures.

articles.title: Malaysia budget 2027: Anwar faces balancing act on cost-of-living relief as general election looms - CNA
articles.summary: Malaysia budget 2027: Anwar faces balancing act on cost-of-living relief as general election looms  CNAINTERACTIVE: Cheaper groceries, bigger tax reliefs and more help for M40 are top wishes for Budget 2027  The StarMalaysian PM Anwar set to boost budget spending as election speculation grows  The Straits TimesRafizi to present Bersama's shadow budget tonight  MalaysiakiniBersama’s budget proposal is a breath of fresh air  Free Malaysia Today
articles.full_text:
Middle-income households are expected to get greater attention, even as economists warn that electoral pressures could slow politically difficult fiscal reforms.
KUALA LUMPUR: With the 2027 budget potentially being Malaysia’s final fiscal blueprint before the 16th general elections (GE16), Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim faces a delicate economic and political balancing act: delivering meaningful cost-of-living relief without undermining fiscal discipline or alienating voters through costly reforms. 
Economists expect Anwar’s government to put greater emphasis on supporting middle-income earners alongside lower-income households, while taking a more cautious approach to politically sensitive reforms as the electoral clock ticks down.
The budget comes after Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) suffered heavy setbacks in the Johor and Negeri Sembilan state elections this year, adding to political pressure on his administration ahead of GE16, which must be held by February 2028.
Economist Anthony Dass of the FSG advisory group told CNA that while the budget was likely to place greater emphasis on immediate households concerns, he did not expect it to be dominated by broad-based short-term handouts.
“The government still has to balance support for the rakyat (public) with fiscal consolidation, structural reforms and measures to strengthen longer-term economic growth,” he said.
“I expect Budget 2027 to be more people-focused, but not necessarily an election giveaway budget.”
The budget - the fifth under the current administration - will be tabled on Friday (Oct 9) at 3.30pm by Anwar, who is also finance minister.
RELIEF TO MOVE BEYOND LOWER-INCOME HOUSEHOLDS?
Economists expect middle-income households, known in Malaysia as the M40 (middle 40 per cent), to receive greater attention in the budget alongside continued support for lower-income groups.
Lee Hwok Aun, a senior fellow and co-coordinator of the Malaysia Studies Programme at ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, told CNA that "emphatic commitments" to cash assistance - some targeted at low- to middle-income households and some universal for all Malaysian adults - can be expected. 
JPMorgan Chase said in a report that the M40 had moved up the cost-of-living agenda, with Anwar making the group a central focus.
“Budget 2027 puts greater attention on the M40 squeeze alongside continued support for lower-income households,” read the paper.
It said that as the subsidy rationalisation continued for the RON95 petrol, it expected savings to be partly redirected towards targeted assistance and measures addressing recurring costs across food, housing, transport, healthcare, education and childcare.
The finance ministry highlighted support for the middle class in its Aug 18 pre-budget statement, including RM150 (US$37) in student schooling aid and two RM100 cash grants for all adults nationwide.
The ministry also emphasised tax breaks targeted at the middle class, such as exemptions for first-home purchases, expanded insurance premium deductions for children, and tax relief for early childhood education (up to RM3,000) and special needs therapy (up to RM10,000).
Analysts stress that such safety nets will be vital to buffer against incoming economic headwinds.
Economist Sedek Jantan of IPP, a financial planning group in Malaysia, said targeted assistance could become more important if a stronger El Nino in 2027 puts further strain on food production and prices.
“This could put renewed pressure on household purchasing power. However, the key question is whether these measures are fiscally sustainable,” he told CNA.
“I would expect the focus to increasingly be on targeted assistance rather than broad-based measures, so that support reaches those who need it most without creating a persistent burden on government finances.”
That constraint remains important even as government spending rises. UOB projects expenditure to reach a record RM445.9 billion - equivalent to 19.6 per cent of the GDP - while the fiscal deficit narrows to 3.3 per cent of GDP from an estimated 3.5 per cent this year.
“This would reinforce the government’s commitment to gradual fiscal consolidation, striking a balance between supporting growth and preserving medium- to long-term fiscal sustainability,” UOB said.
REFORMS CONTINUE, BUT HOW FAR WITH GE16 LOOMING?
Economists told CNA that while reforms will continue, they are likely to proceed at a more cautious pace.
Sedek said that the government could not afford to completely put structural reforms on hold, but expected a more calibrated and carefully sequenced approach, particularly for measures that directly impact household incomes and business costs.
He said the government could further tighten eligibility for subsidies and reduce leakages before making more substantial adjustments.
On revenue, Sedek does not expect major new taxes on individuals or companies, with the government likely to focus instead on improving tax compliance, broadening the effective tax base and strengthening collection.
Anwar said in August that the finance ministry was studying a proposal to create a hybrid tax system combining features of the Sales and Service Tax (SST) and the Goods and Services Tax (GST).  
Dass also said reforms will continue, but added it was politically difficult to introduce measures that impose visible additional costs on households. 
“I don’t expect the government to abandon structural reforms, but I do expect the pace and sequencing to become more cautious,” he said.
Others believe the political window for more painful reforms is closing.
Lee of ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute said major structural reforms were becoming politically risky, particularly further subsidy rationalisation that would fully or partially float prices.
He noted that the government had already scaled back plans to progressively target fuel subsidies, opting instead to retain the full subsidy for all Malaysians up to a monthly limit rather than reduce support for higher-income earners.
“Such reforms are less and less likely, the closer we get to the next election,” he said.
Aira Azhari, the CEO of the Institute for Democracy and Economic Affairs (IDEAS), echoed this, saying that further rationalisation of petrol subsidies was unlikely, pointing to the government's recent decision to restore the monthly subsidised RON95 quota for Malaysians to 300 litres.
“It is too politically risky to introduce any other subsidy rationalisation in this budget,” she told CNA.
In August, Anwar announced that the government would restore a quota for Malaysian citizens to buy the popular RON95 transport fuel to 300 litres per month, after reducing it to 200 litres a month earlier this year amid a surge in global crude oil prices due to the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The quota for diesel purchases for certain categories of users would be similarly raised to 400 litres per month.
SHORT-TERM RELIEF VS LONGER-TERM VALUE
Economists also cautioned against allowing short-term cost-of-living measures to come at the expense of investment, productivity and longer-term reforms.
In this light, Sedek said the approaching general election would inevitably increase pressure on the government to address issues voters felt most directly, including the cost of living, incomes and essential services.
But he said the government needed to distinguish between measures that provide “immediate emotional reassurance” and those that create lasting economic value.
“Some low-hanging-fruit measures may provide quick relief and be well-received by households, but they are not necessarily sustainable if they create recurring fiscal commitments without improving productivity, wages or income-generating capacity,” he said.
Stewart Nixon, director of research at IDEAS, similarly warned that the budget is being drawn up under the shadow of looming polls, with "election budgets" historically prioritising short-term political expediency over long-term investment and structural reform.
“Governments typically tinker with and throw more money at existing policies, particularly in contested electorates, rather than pursue systemic change to address the people’s most pressing needs,” he wrote in a statement on Oct 6.
Dass said the government should also focus less on announcing new programmes and more on whether existing measures were producing results.
“Malaysia already has many programmes, incentives, grants and financing schemes. The question should now be: what did we achieve from them?" he said.
"Did productivity improve? Did SMEs grow? Did investments create better jobs? Did wages rise? Did household purchasing power improve?"

News analysis
Indonesia’s efforts are keeping the terror threat under control, but can it continue to stay ahead?
AI generated
JAKARTA – Scattered across Indonesia’s sprawling archipelago, suspected militants affiliated to Daulah Islamiah were quietly seeking one another out. Not just through clandestine meetings, but also from behind computer screens.
They collaborated online to recruit followers, spread extremist teachings and rebuilt networks across provincial lines. Some had also allegedly undergone weapons training, suggesting their activities could eventually have progressed to attacks.
They did not get that far. Densus 88, Indonesia’s counterterrorism squad, said on Oct 4 it had arrested 11 suspects across six provinces over the previous two days – demonstrating a proactive approach which has kept Indonesia free from terrorist attacks for nearly four years.
While the militants’ target profiles are not clear, IS affiliates in Indonesia had attacked government installations and places of worship in the past.
The arrests reflect how years of disruption through counter-terrorism efforts have weakened Indonesia’s militant networks and delivered significant security gains, analysts said.
But they said the latest sweep also shows how extremists are adapting, using digital spaces to recruit, reconnect and rebuild after prominent organised terrorist groups in the country became demobilised.
Notably, Jemaah Islamiyah (JI), the Al-Qaeda-linked group behind the 2002 Bali bombings, disbanded in 2024 after years of pressure. High-profile JI members were not arrested in the recent cycles of terrorist arrests, suggesting the group might be living up to its promise of moving away from violence, although the authorities remain cautious. Some of its leaders continue to serve long jail sentences.

The authorities have also severely weakened the pro-Islamic State, Jemaah Ansharut Daulah (JAD), whose members carried out a series of suicide bombings targeting churches and police in Surabaya in May 2018. The attacks, some involving entire families and their children, killed 15 people, excluding 13 attackers.
The last terrorist attack in Indonesia was a suicide bombing at a police station in Bandung in December 2022 by a JAD operative that killed one officer and injured 10 others.
The decline in terrorist violence in Indonesia is part of a broader global trend. The 2026 Global Terrorism Index, produced by the Australia-based Institute for Economics and Peace, found that deaths from terrorism worldwide fell 28% in 2025 to 5,582, while the number of attacks dropped 22% to 2,944 – the lowest levels recorded since 2007.
The longer-term decline follows a peak in terrorism deaths in 2015, with the index pointing to major counter-terrorism successes in Iraq, Syria and the wider Middle East as contributing factors. These included the military defeat of the Islamic State’s territorial caliphate, which once controlled large areas of Iraq and Syria.
The relative calm in Indonesia in the last few years, not an easy feat given the vastness of the country and its population, along with a history of militant activities in parts of the country and in neighbouring Philippines, has required repeated interventions. These include close monitoring of suspects and networks, timely arrests of members belonging to large networks, awareness campaigns and deradicalisation drives.
The authorities say they have thwarted about 28 terrorist plots in the last four years.
Alif Satria, a research fellow at the International Centre for Political Violence and Terrorism Research (ICPVTR), S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS), said the success of Indonesia’s counter-terror efforts are not only owed to the timely apprehension of would-be attackers, but also through the systematic targeting of the larger enabling eco-system that comprises propagandists, trainers and recruiters.
“By disrupting these supporting networks alongside operational members, the authorities can significantly constrain an organisation’s ability to sustain its activities,” he said.
A 2018 revision of the country’s terrorism law gave the authorities greater scope to act during the preparation and planning stages, allowing Densus 88 to disrupt plots and the networks supporting them before violence occurs.
Muh Taufiqurrohman, a senior researcher at the Jakarta-based Centre for Radicalism and Deradicalisation Studies, said Densus 88 has become more methodical in building cases, with investigators holding case conferences and requiring at least two pieces of evidence against a suspect before an arrest.
Soft approaches but not going soft
Analysts say the gains have come from more than arrests alone. The authorities have increasingly calibrated their response according to the level of threat.
Taufiqurrohman pointed to one recent set of cases involving 24 teenagers exposed to violent extremist communities. Only one was detained, while the others underwent assessments and counselling, with their families brought into the intervention, suggesting openness to case-specific approaches where warranted.
Just days before the latest arrests, Densus 88 held an “ideological transformation” programme in Banten aimed at reinforcing former JI members’ move away from extremism and helping them reintegrate into society.
Former senior JI figures Para Wijayanto and Zarkasih were among the speakers, while participants watched a film reflecting on the first year since JI’s dissolution and took part in discussions on moderate Islam, national values and the rejection of violent ideology.
Densus 88 said it had conducted 19 such programmes across Indonesia, working with local governments, religious leaders and other groups to help former JI members reintegrate into their communities.
Adlini Ilma Ghaisany Sjah, an associate research fellow with RSIS’ ICPVTR, said Indonesia’s record reflected a combination of “hard” and “soft” approaches.
“The soft approach shows the government engaging in dialogue with incarcerated terrorists, supporting civil society organisations and community- based preventing and countering violent extremism (PCVE) programmes, and assisting rehabilitation and reintegration.
“Indonesia has used soft approach policies since the mid-2000s, but the measures became more integrated after the establishment of the BNPT (National Counter-Terrorism Agency) in 2010 and the introduction of the National Action Plan on PCVE in 2021,” she added.
Alif observed that years of arrests had steadily eroded the organisational capacity of Indonesia’s major militant groups, disrupting their leadership as well as the recruitment, propaganda and training networks that sustained them.
But while the fragmentation of Indonesia’s militant landscape has made large, coordinated attacks harder to organise, it has also created smaller networks that can be harder to detect because they leave fewer organisational and communication trails.
The latest arrests point to another shift: attempts to bring some of those fragments back together.
“What these latest IS-linked arrests show is that there are still efforts at consolidating and centralising the network,” Adlini said.
Online dangers persist
A bigger long-term concern is how militant networks are finding new ways to reach young people, as the pathways into extremism increasingly extend beyond conventional ideological recruitment.
In September, the BNPT said 620 children aged 11 to 18 across 34 provinces had been exposed to violent and radical narratives online between January and August.
Densus 88 has raised concerns about other online pathways through which young people can be exposed to violence. In January, the unit said it had identified 70 children aged 11 to 18 across 19 provinces who were members of so-called True Crime Communities (TCC), an online subculture centred on real-life violent crimes and their perpetrators.
Adlini said these communities differ from Islamist militant groups such as JAD, which have clearer ideological narratives and identifiable leaders. TCCs, on the other hand, are leaderless, drawing young people through violent imagery, notoriety or a sense of belonging rather than a coherent ideology.
Experts worry that extremist recruiters could tap into these primed young people already immersed in violent online spaces, and that the progression from fascination with violence to extremist intent can be rapid.
Taufiqurrohman cited one pro-Islamic State youth who went from encountering a gore video on TikTok to planning attacks on Parliament and a police station within about three months.
As the youth became more deeply immersed in extremist content, he was drawn into WhatsApp groups that together had around 1,660 members, some administered using foreign phone numbers.
AI could further shorten their pathway to violence. Taufiqurrohman said his research found pro-Islamic State youths in Indonesia using AI tools like ChatGPT alongside other more widely accessible online and communication tools to reinforce their beliefs.

Myanmar’s junta chief-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing arrived in Malaysia yesterday for talks with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, as the military-backed leader once shunned by regional nations seeks international legitimacy.
The two-day visit comes as Malaysia pushes ahead with a controversial move to repatriate thousands of Myanmar nationals, despite warnings from the UN and rights groups that returnees could face serious danger amid a raging civil war.
“The visit provides the prime minister with an opportunity to sustain his direct engagement with Myanmar,” the Malaysian government said in a statement on Tuesday.

Key bilateral issues include the “voluntary, dignified and safe repatriation of Myanmar nationals of all ethnic groups who have been in Malaysia illegally,” it added.
Myanmar has been in turmoil since Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup in 2021, triggering a nationwide civil war that has killed an estimated 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million.
The military engineered a widely criticized election that allowed Min Aung Hlaing, who is subject to a raft of Western sanctions, to take up a civilian role — a transition that has sparked some moves toward re-engagement with Myanmar.
Although Min Aung Hlaing and other senior Myanmar officials have been excluded from ASEAN summits since 2021 over their failure to implement a peace road map brokered by the group, individual countries in the region have moved to rebuild ties with Naypyitaw.
Since formally becoming president in April, Min Aung Hlaing has visited ASEAN members Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam, and also made trips to China, India, Russia and Belarus.
In Malaysia, following a wave of online hate speech and misinformation earlier this year, pressure on undocumented migrants and refugees has grown, particularly against Rohingya Muslims, many of whom fled a brutal 2017 military crackdown in Myanmar’s Rakhine state bordering Bangladesh.
Last month, Anwar said in a podcast that he would invite Min Aung Hlaing for an official visit if Myanmar accepted the return of thousands of Rohingya refugees.
“Under pressure to send refugees back, Anwar needs Naypyitaw’s cooperation, and a visit is the price,” International Crisis Group senior Asia adviser Richard Horsey said. “He says this is not recognition, but Min Aung Hlaing will present it as exactly that.”
Fortify Rights senior human rights specialist Yap Lay Sheng agreed, saying that the Migrant returns are the “only reason” Malaysia wants to engage with Myanmar.
“For so many years Malaysia has shown the military regime the cold shoulder,” he said. “Suddenly there’s a 180 degree about turn to welcome the regime with open arms.”
Malaysia has deported about 10,000 Myanmar nationals since January, according to Anwar, who said Burmese authorities had given assurances those returning would not be harmed.
Although Malaysia has said the repatriations are strictly voluntary, the UN has raised concerns about the move, warning that people sent back to Myanmar might face serious risks.
Rights groups have also urged Malaysia to halt the returns, citing the ongoing violence and risk of forced conscription.
Despite repeated calls for an end to the violence, including from ASEAN, the civil war in Myanmar continues unabated.
The Burmese military has carried out several airstrikes within the last fortnight in Rakhine, where it is battling a rebel group, killing at least 58 people and injuring dozens of others, including at a busy market.
The attack was the deadliest since a hospital bombing in December and drew condemnation from UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.
ASEAN’s current chair, the Philippines, also expressed concern over the airstrike.

Google wants to deepen its partnership with Vietnam and contribute to the country’s artificial intelligence development goals, a senior global executive said.
During a meeting with Vietnamese Deputy Prime Minister Ho Quoc Dung on Monday, Cris Turner, vice president of knowledge & information products, government affairs and public policy at Google, said the company is seeking effective ways to expand cooperation with Vietnam, particularly in AI,
Turner said Google wants its cooperation to deliver practical benefits for Vietnamese people. He also discussed Vietnam’s development potential, international experience, and possible areas for cooperation to strengthen economic, trade, and investment ties between Vietnam and the U.S.
In reply, Deputy PM Dung stressed that Vietnam considers science-technology, innovation, and digital transformation key drivers of economic growth.
The country’s market size, demographic structure, and increasingly dynamic technology business community provide a foundation for Vietnam to develop into a regional hub for technology development and applications, he said.
Vietnam is seeking partnerships that combine investment with research and development, technology transfer, and high-quality workforce training, Dung said. The goal is to strengthen domestic companies and help them develop products capable of competing in global markets.
He called on Google to continue supporting Vietnam’s digital ecosystem and help “Make in Vietnam” products and solutions expand into international markets. Vietnam welcomes U.S. investment, particularly in science, technology, and digital transformation, he underscored.
Google has maintained a presence in Vietnam since opening its Ho Chi Minh City office in 2023. In AI, Google has worked with the National Innovation Center (NIC) since July 2024 under the “AI Vietnam Future” initiative. The program covered 40,000 scholarships for digital skills training, including AI courses, as well as support programs for startups.
In June 2025, Google and NIC expanded their cooperation with initiatives aimed at supporting AI startups and promoting AI literacy in Vietnam.

articles.title: The pace of interest rate increases is slowing down. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The pace of interest rate increases is slowing down.  Vietnam.vn

Speaking at a press conference, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam, Pham Thanh Ha, said that with the synchronized solutions of the State Bank of Vietnam, the rate of interest rate increase is slowing down and the interest rate level is basically revolving around a new level. By September 20, 2026, the average deposit interest rate for new transactions will be 6.38%/year, an increase of 1.15%/year compared to the end of 2025.
 By the end of September , credit had increased by 16.69% compared to the same period last year.
 In his opening remarks at the press conference, the Deputy Governor stated that 2026 is the first year of implementing the Resolution of the 14th National Congress of the Party, and also the first year of implementing the 5-year socio -economic development plan 2026-2030, striving for double-digit growth while maintaining macroeconomic stability, controlling inflation, and ensuring the major balances of the economy. 
|  | 
| Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam, Pham Thanh Ha, speaks at the press conference. | 
 In the early months of 2026, the global landscape continued to be complex and unpredictable. Geopolitical tensions, particularly the escalating conflict in the Middle East, put significant pressure on international commodity and financial markets, leading to soaring oil prices and supply chain disruptions.
 Central banks are reacting more cautiously to the risk of renewed inflation, with some raising interest rates: on September 16, the US Federal Reserve (FED) decided to raise interest rates by 0.25%, bringing the federal funds rate to the 3.75%-4.00% range; the European Central Bank (ECB) on September 10 decided to raise key interest rates by 0.25 percentage points - this is the second time the ECB has raised interest rates in 2026; the Bank of Japan (BOJ) on September 18 decided to raise its policy interest rate from 1% to 1.25%, the highest level in 31 years.
 High interest rates coupled with safe-haven demand have caused the US dollar to rebound strongly after a period of downward correction earlier in the year. These developments are putting pressure on the monetary policy management of emerging and developing economies with high levels of openness, such as Vietnam.
 In that context, according to the Deputy Governor, under the leadership of the Party, the decisive direction of the Government and the Prime Minister , and the efforts of ministries, sectors, localities, the business community, and the people, the socio-economic situation in September and the first nine months of 2026 in our country continued to improve positively. Macroeconomics remained stable, inflation was under control, major balances were ensured, and various sectors and fields achieved many important results, with each month and each quarter better than the previous one, creating momentum for growth in the remaining months of 2026.
 Statistics show that GDP growth in the third quarter reached 9.95% year-on-year, approaching double digits. For the first nine months of the year, GDP growth is estimated at 9.01%, the highest in the past 15 years. These figures provide a solid foundation for double-digit economic growth for the entire year of 2026, preparing the groundwork for 2027 and subsequent years.
 The Consumer Price Index (CPI) in September increased by 0.62% compared to the previous month and by 5.08% compared to the same period last year; the average CPI for the first nine months of 2026 increased by 4.52% compared to the same period last year. These are the highest increases for September and the nine-month average in many years, indicating significant pressure on price management in the remaining months of 2026.
 In the first nine months of 2026, the State Bank of Vietnam proactively and flexibly managed monetary policy, closely coordinating with a reasonable and focused expansionary fiscal policy and other macroeconomic policies to steadfastly prioritize the target of controlling inflation in 2026 at an average of approximately 4.5%, contributing to maintaining macroeconomic stability and supporting sustainable economic growth.
 Specifically, the State Bank of Vietnam has flexibly managed open market operations, in line with market developments, contributing to the stability of the monetary market and the achievement of monetary policy objectives. As a result, the payment and disbursement needs of credit institutions have been ensured and smooth, and interest rates in the interbank market have tended to decrease.
 Regarding interest rate management, the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) faced significant pressure but implemented decisive measures to stabilize market interest rates in order to support businesses and individuals. Specifically, it continued to maintain the policy interest rates to facilitate access to low-cost capital from the SBV for credit institutions; directed credit institutions to implement solutions to stabilize interest rates and required them to continue publishing lending interest rate information on their websites for customers to refer to when accessing loans; applied technology; and promoted digital transformation . It also directed regional SBV branches to hold meetings with commercial bank branches in their areas to check the implementation of interest rate reductions as directed by the SBV. 
|  | 
| Overview of the press conference | 
 “With the above solutions, the rate of interest rate increase is slowing down and the interest rate level is basically revolving around the new level. By September 20, 2026, the average deposit interest rate for new transactions will be 6.38%/year, an increase of 1.15%/year compared to the end of 2025,” the Deputy Governor informed.
 Regarding exchange rate management, the exchange rate and foreign exchange market are under pressure from complex and unpredictable developments in the international market and domestic challenges and difficulties. In this context, the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) manages the exchange rate flexibly, contributing to the stability of the foreign exchange market, macroeconomic stability, and inflation control. As a result, the foreign exchange market operates smoothly, the legitimate foreign currency needs of the economy are met fully and promptly; and the USD/VND exchange rate fluctuates flexibly, in line with market conditions.
 In managing credit, the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) continues to implement appropriate credit management solutions to contribute to controlling inflation, stabilizing the macroeconomy, and supporting economic growth. The SBV has promptly and transparently announced the principles for assigning credit growth targets for 2026 to enable credit institutions to proactively implement them. Simultaneously, during the management process, the SBV has implemented solutions to create room for credit institutions to provide credit for certain important needs serving economic growth and to facilitate credit provision for certain types of real estate in line with the Party and State's policies, such as: Not including the additional credit outstanding compared to the end of 2025 for social housing, industrial parks, export processing zones; restaurants, hotels, tourist areas, ecological and resort areas in the credit outstanding for the real estate sector when controlling real estate credit growth.

 In addition, the State Bank of Vietnam promptly directed credit institutions to implement credit solutions for a number of industries and sectors, creating favorable conditions for businesses and people to access credit; and actively implemented the directives of the Government and the Prime Minister in providing capital for large-scale and key projects.
 On the part of credit institutions, they have actively disbursed funds for credit programs as directed by the Government, the Prime Minister, and the State Bank of Vietnam, such as the credit program for forestry and fisheries sectors, which has increased in scale from VND 15,000 billion to VND 185,000 billion; the loan program for linking production, processing, and consumption of high-quality, low-emission rice products in the Mekong Delta has been vigorously implemented, and timely coordination with the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment has been carried out to resolve difficulties and obstacles arising during implementation.

SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE, October 7th, 2026, Chainwire
Canton Forum Singapore will convene institutions, digital asset leaders, technology providers and ecosystem builders to explore the next phase of on-chain finance in Asia
Canton Foundation, the independent organization supporting the development and adoption of the Canton Network, will host Canton Forum Singapore on October 8 at the ArtScience Museum, bringing together participants from across finance, digital assets, technology and the broader Canton ecosystem.
Held during TOKEN2049 week, Canton Forum will explore how traditional finance, digital assets and decentralized markets are increasingly converging and what that means for the future of financial markets in Asia and globally.
As tokenization moves beyond experimentation, the conversation is also changing. The question is no longer simply whether financial assets can be brought on-chain, but how those assets can interact, access liquidity, settle and move across different markets and applications.
“Asia is becoming one of the most important regions shaping the future of global financial markets,” said Viv Diwakar, Head of the Canton Foundation. “We are moving beyond the question of whether assets can be brought on-chain. The focus now is on how those assets can interact, settle and move across markets at institutional scale, while meeting the requirements of regulated finance. Canton Forum brings together the institutions, innovators and ecosystem participants working through those questions today and Singapore is a natural place to have that conversation.” 
The program will open with remarks from Yuval Rooz, Co-Founder and CEO of Digital Asset, followed by a series of conversations examining some of the most important shifts taking place across financial markets today from Asia’s move from tokenization experiments toward institutional adoption, to the growing convergence of traditional finance, DeFi and digital assets, and Singapore’s role as a regional hub for tokenized capital markets.
Bringing together perspectives from across finance, digital assets, technology and the Canton ecosystem, the discussions will explore what comes next as on-chain markets mature including how assets can move across applications, access liquidity and connect with existing financial infrastructure.
The Forum will conclude with remarks from Viv Diwakar, Head of the Canton Foundation, before transitioning into a dedicated networking session bringing together institutions, digital
asset companies, technology providers, builders, investors and members of the broader ecosystem.
Connecting a Growing Financial Ecosystem Canton Forum reflects a broader evolution taking place across the industry.
Financial institutions are exploring tokenized securities, funds, collateral, payments and settlement. Digital asset companies are creating new forms of liquidity and distribution. Technology providers and builders are developing the infrastructure and applications needed to connect these markets.
Increasingly, these developments cannot happen in isolation.
The Canton Network is designed to enable financial applications and assets to interoperate while allowing participants to maintain the privacy, control and governance required for institutional financial activity.
For Canton Foundation, Asia-Pacific is an increasingly important part of that ecosystem, with Singapore serving as a key hub for supporting engagement and growth across the region.
“Some of the most significant work in digital finance is now happening across Asia,” said Diwakar. “Singapore sits at the intersection of global capital, financial institutions, technology and regulatory innovation. Bringing Canton Forum here reflects both the importance of the market and our commitment to building a broader ecosystem across the region as financial markets increasingly move on-chain.” 
Canton Forum Singapore will take place on October 8, 2026, at the ArtScience Museum, Singapore, from 1:00 p.m. to 9:00 p.m.

articles.title: Melaka to head to the polls on Nov 14 in another test of shifting political alliances in Malaysia - CNA
articles.summary: Melaka to head to the polls on Nov 14 in another test of shifting political alliances in Malaysia  CNAMalacca BN firm on 21 seats, open to swaps; state Harapan to go solo  MalaysiakiniMelaka state election: Parties split over Nov 14 polling date  The Straits TimesAnalysts: Festive break unlikely to deter Melaka voters  The StarMalaysia’s Melaka sets election date as BN, PAS near alliance against Anwar  South China Morning Post
articles.full_text:
MELAKA: Nearly 700,000 voters in Melaka are set to cast their ballots in the state polls on Nov 14, the Election Commission (EC) announced on Wednesday (Oct 7), in another test of shifting political alliances ahead of Malaysia's next general election.
The election period will run for 14 days after the nomination of candidates on Oct 31, with early voting set for Nov 10.
Melaka Chief Minister Ab Rauf Yusoh had announced the official dissolution of the state legislative assembly on Sep 23, paving the way for an election that was otherwise due by February 2027.
Before the dissolution, the state government was led by the Barisan Nasional (BN) coalition.
In the 2021 state election, BN won 21 of the 28 seats, while Pakatan Harapan (PH) secured five seats and Perikatan Nasional (PN) claimed two seats.
PH joined the state government in 2023 when Ab Rauf became chief minister and reshuffled the executive council to reflect the PH-BN partnership at the federal level following the 2022 general election that had resulted in a hung parliament.
PH however withdrew its support for the state government in July in protest against a constitutional amendment allowing for the appointment of nominated assemblymen.
It is still unclear who the various political coalitions will pick as their partners for the upcoming Melaka polls.
BN chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said on Sunday that negotiations with potential partners were about 95 per cent complete, with the coalition expected to announce the outcome after the election date is revealed on Wednesday.
There are 687,697 registered voters in Melaka as of Sep 22, 2026. They comprise 675,166 ordinary voters, 9,769 military personnel and their spouses and 2,762 police personnel, the EC said in a statement on Wednesday.
A total of 271 polling centres will be set up, with 11,175 people mobilised to facilitate the state election.
The election will need an estimated allocation of RM28.45 million (US$6.96 million), according to the EC.
The upcoming polls in Melaka come just months after BN’s landslide victories in the Negeri Sembilan and Johor state elections.
It won 25 of 36 seats in Negeri Sembilan on Aug 1 as part of a pact with the opposition PN, and 48 of 56 seats in the Johor state election in July where it had contested solo.
While BN and PN’s dominant party, the Parti Islam Se-Malaysia (PAS) cooperated in Negeri Sembilan, their leaders have not agreed on how they would contest in Melaka.
BN has reportedly said it will defend all seats it won in the last polls, but PAS has said it plans to contest 16 of Melaka’s 28 seats, including Tanjung Bidara, which is led by BN’s Ab Rauf, reported local media.
As for Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s PH, its Melaka chapter is finalising negotiations, including with Bersatu, to form a “PH Plus” collaboration, local media previously reported.
Analysts earlier told CNA that they would be keeping an eye on who BN works with in Melaka, or if it goes solo, noting that it would be another challenge for Anwar and PH, who have not recovered from their defeats in Johor and Negeri Sembilan.
Another factor that could shape the campaign is the Malaysian king’s decision on Sep 18 to allow former Malaysia prime minister Najib Razak to serve the remainder of his prison sentence under house arrest, conditional on him paying a RM50 million (US$12.26 million) fine.
Analysts earlier told CNA that Najib’s conditional pardon could give a boost to BN, given the influence the 73-year-old still wields there.
The Melaka polls come as Malaysia’s political alliances continue to shift ahead of the next general election. The 16th General Election must be held by February 2028, although Anwar has said he is open to considering calls for an earlier vote.
